arXiv:2611.01899v1 [cond-mat.str-el] 01 Nov 2026

Disorder, Interactions, and the Fate of the
Two-Dimensional Electron System:
Wigner Crystal, Metal-Insulator Transition, and Amorphous Solid

Sankar Das Sarma Affiliation: Condensed Matter Theory Center and Joint Quantum Institute, Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of Maryland, Affiliation: College Park, Maryland 20742, USA Email: dassarma@umd.edu
November 1, 2026
Abstract

We present a unified theoretical study of the interplay between Coulomb disorder and Coulomb interactions in two-dimensional electron systems, covering the Wigner crystallization transition, the metal-insulator transition, and the crossover from a Wigner crystal to an amorphous localized solid in both zero magnetic field and the lowest Landau level. Using Hartree-Fock theory, variational Monte Carlo, and percolation and strong-localization arguments, we show that quenched charged disorder destroys true long-range Wigner crystalline order in the thermodynamic limit at any nonzero charged-impurity density, within the Imry-Ma-Larkin framework; the finite-system density image is that of an amorphous solid with crystalline coherence over at most a few lattice spacings. For the two-dimensional metal–insulator transition we show, in a controlled nonlinear-Thomas–Fermi model of long-range Coulomb disorder at setback dd, that the half-depletion density of the semiclassical landscape and the Ioffe–Regel–Mott density of Born–RPA transport track each other to within a factor of order unity over the physically relevant range of impurity density and setback, with a slow ni−1/10d−1/5n_{i}^{-1/10}d^{-1/5} spread; the agreement reflects the common energy scale Edis∼EFE_{\mathrm{dis}}\sim E_{F} at the transition rather than a theorem, and modest independent short-range transport channels can shift the ratio by factors of order two. The article is a theoretical study under well-defined approximations; it takes the recent scanning tunneling microscopy imaging experiments on two-dimensional electron systems and the longstanding disorder-versus-interaction debate on the two-dimensional metal–insulator transition as motivation, and leaves to the reader the comparison between its calculated signatures and the published experimental analyses.

1 Introduction

A two-dimensional (2D) electron system crystallizes when the Coulomb energy sufficiently dominates the kinetic energy, that is, when the dimensionless density parameter rs=1/(π​n​aB∗)r_{s}=1/(\sqrt{\pi n}\,a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}) exceeds a critical value rcr_{c}. Quantum Monte Carlo places rcr_{c} in the range of a few tens, with the specific value depending on the spin sector and the trial-wave-function family used [1, 2, 3, 4]; Drummond and Needs [3] report the clean paramagnetic-fluid to antiferromagnetic-crystal transition at rc=31​(1)r_{c}=31(1), with the ferromagnetic crystal becoming stable at a different density. The spin sector relevant to a given calculation therefore matters when quoting an rcr_{c}. This number is a property of the interacting electrons alone: it is the density below which the interaction-driven spontaneous breaking of continuous translational symmetry becomes energetically favorable. Throughout this paper aa denotes the average inter-particle separation, which is also, up to a numerical factor of order unity, the lattice constant of the pristine triangular Wigner crystal at the same density. Hartree–Fock (HF) theory, which neglects correlation, places the crystallization transition at a lower rsr_{s} than the quantum many-body result; a commensurate HF search puts the transition at rs≃2.65r_{s}\simeq 2.65 in the fully spin-polarized gas [5, 6, 7]. In the lowest Landau level, where kinetic energy is quenched and the entire problem is the projected Coulomb interaction, HF produces a Wigner crystal at every partial filling ν<1\nu<1 [8, 9, 10, 11].

The physical question that this paper addresses is what happens to this interaction-driven crystallization in the presence of quenched Coulomb disorder. The motivation is twofold. First, recent scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) experiments on gate-tunable monolayer and bilayer MoSe2 [12, 13, 14, 15] and on Bernal bilayer graphene in a strong perpendicular field [16] report real-space density images that are interpreted as Wigner solids. In the zero-field experiments these images are obtained at electron densities corresponding to rs≲20r_{s}\lesssim 20, well inside the clean quantum liquid regime, and the solid-like appearance becomes more robust as the short-range disorder density is increased [13]. The experimental groups [13, 14] and parts of the theoretical literature [17, 18, 19] discuss the disorder-stabilized Wigner-solid picture. The present paper addresses, within a specific set of microscopic approximations, an alternative structural picture [20]: that at rs<rcr_{s}<r_{c} a correlated electron state can be organized by a quenched impurity landscape into an amorphous solid whose density pattern resembles a solid locally while lacking true long-range crystalline order. Which picture is the correct description of a given imaged sample is a question for the experimental analysis; the role of the present paper is to work out what the amorphous-solid picture predicts quantitatively within Hartree–Fock, variational Monte Carlo, and lowest-Landau-level Hartree–Fock, and to set out the structural observables that distinguish it from a disorder-broken Wigner crystal.

Second, the metal–insulator transition (MIT) in two dimensions has been debated for more than three decades. Scaling theory predicts that all states in a 2D disordered system are localized at any disorder, which would preclude a true metallic phase at T=0T=0. Experimentally [21], however, 2D electron systems in Si MOSFETs and in GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructures exhibit a low-temperature resistivity that decreases with decreasing temperature on the metallic side of a critical carrier density ncn_{c}, and increases on the insulating side. Two mutually exclusive-looking theoretical pictures have been proposed for the transition: (i) classical percolation through a disorder-induced puddle landscape [22, 23, 24, 25], where ncn_{c} is identified as the density at which the connected region of the self-consistent electron density first spans the sample; and (ii) a quantum Ioffe–Regel–Mott (IRM) strong-localization crossover, where ncn_{c} is identified as the density at which kF​ℓMFP∼1k_{F}\ell_{\rm MFP}\sim 1 [26, 27, 28, 29]. The empirical observation is that the two definitions give the same ncn_{c} to within a numerical factor of order unity, over a range of disorder strengths and setback distances. Why they should coincide is a quantitative question with no obvious a priori answer.

The two topics—whether a 2D electron solid can be interaction-driven or impurity-driven, and what controls the critical density of the 2D MIT—are facets of the same underlying problem: how do Coulomb interactions and Coulomb disorder compete to organize the electrons in two dimensions, and which of them wins at which density, and at which disorder strength. This paper studies that competition with a battery of complementary microscopic methods: self-consistent Hartree–Fock theory of a periodic 16-electron supercell at zero field; variational Monte Carlo (VMC) with N=16N=16 spin-polarized electrons at rs=10r_{s}=10, 2020, 3030, 5050 in three disorder models; Hartree–Fock on a torus in the lowest Landau level; and nonlinear Thomas–Fermi (TF) screening with explicit computation of the percolation threshold and the Ioffe–Regel–Mott density. The results are compared with the quantum HF and classical molecular dynamics (MD) study of Das Sarma and Pan [30], which uses a different disorder model and arrives at a consistent picture.

The main organizing variable throughout the paper is the dimensionless disorder-to-electron density ratio

ηdis≡n¯i/n,\eta_{\mathrm{dis}}\equiv\bar{n}_{i}/n, (1)

where n¯i\bar{n}_{i} is the density of charged impurities seen by the 2D electron gas (including, for Coulomb impurities at setback dd, the appropriate screening function; the explicit form appears in Sec. 5). The reason for this choice is already clear on general grounds and is derived in detail in Secs. 2 and 3: at rs<rcr_{s}<r_{c} the clean system is a correlated liquid, and whether its density image looks solid is controlled by the ratio of the disorder energy to the Coulomb repulsion scale e2/ae^{2}/a, not by rsr_{s} alone; and at rs>rcr_{s}>r_{c} the clean HF system is a crystal whose coherence is cut off by the random pinning at a scale set by ηdis\eta_{\mathrm{dis}}. In both regimes ηdis\eta_{\mathrm{dis}} decides the outcome.

A note on notation. Because the material of Secs. 2–5 was developed in independent calculations with different natural notational conventions, the symbol for the dimensionless impurity density varies modestly between sections: ni/nn_{i}/n with no bar in the HF and VMC analyses (Secs. 2–3), Ni/NN_{i}/N for the finite LLL torus (Sec. 4), n¯i\bar{n}_{i} with bar in the TF/MIT analysis (Sec. 5) where the spatial-averaged impurity density enters the continuum-Gaussian construction, and c=n¯i/n0c=\bar{n}_{i}/n_{0} in the comparison with Ref. [30] (Sec. 6). These are the same physical quantity. Separately, the dimensionless disorder parameter ηdis≡n¯i/n\eta_{\mathrm{dis}}\equiv\bar{n}_{i}/n of Eq. (1) coincides with the quantity η=W/EF\eta=W/E_{F} used in Sec. 6 only through its definition in each section; the two η\eta’s are not the same variable. The difference in notations in different sections is consistent with the different problems and models being considered in each section although they all bear upon the issue of central conceptual interest: competition between disorder and interaction in 2D electron layers.

A theorem shapes everything that follows. The Imry–Ma–Larkin argument [31, 32, 33] states that a system with a continuous order parameter cannot possess true long-range order in two dimensions in the presence of any nonzero random field: the energy that an arbitrarily weak random field gains by locally following the order-parameter texture, over a region of linear size RR, grows faster with RR than the elastic cost of the texture. For the 2D Wigner crystal, which is characterized by the spontaneous breaking of continuous translational symmetry, this theorem forbids true crystalline Bragg peaks at any nonzero charged disorder. What remains is an amorphous solid: a state with no long-range translational order, but with crystalline coherence over a finite length RcR_{c} (the Larkin length) that is set by the competition between elastic stiffness and random-force variance.

The Larkin theorem has two regimes that must be distinguished. In the weak-pinning (collective) regime Rc≫aR_{c}\gg a, the random field couples linearly to the elastic displacement of a well-formed crystal and the Imry–Ma–Larkin estimate for RcR_{c} is sharp. In the strong-pinning regime Rc∼aR_{c}\sim a, the coupling is to the individual-pinning scale and the elastic description of a crystal breaks down; the state is then more naturally described as a glass of impurity-trapped electrons than as an elastically pinned Wigner crystal. The amorphous solid of Secs. 2–4 sits predominantly in the strong-pinning regime, where the two descriptions agree on the qualitative conclusion (no long-range Bragg order, coherence over at most a few lattice spacings) but on different microscopic grounds. Our finite-system calculations (N=16N=16 and N=36N=36 in Sec. 2; Nϕ≤200N_{\phi}\leq 200 in Sec. 4) resolve coherence lengths at the lattice spacing and up but cannot in principle distinguish Rc=aR_{c}=a from Rc=3​aR_{c}=3a, and we are careful below not to claim otherwise.

A second, physical observation sharpens the picture. Consider a 2D electron system of density nn in a landscape of quenched Coulomb impurities of density n¯i\bar{n}_{i}. At fixed impurity density, lowering nn increases rsr_{s} and also increases ηdis=n¯i/n\eta_{\mathrm{dis}}=\bar{n}_{i}/n. In the limit n≪n¯in\ll\bar{n}_{i} the state is organized by the impurity landscape rather than by mutual Coulomb repulsion: there are more pinning centers than electrons, and the electrons occupy a subset of the attractive wells (fewer electrons than wells, so not every well is filled). In the opposite limit n¯i≪n\bar{n}_{i}\ll n the state is a weakly disordered correlated liquid. Across the (rs,ηdis)(r_{s},\eta_{\mathrm{dis}}) plane sampled by the microscopic calculations of Secs. 2–4, weak-disorder changes to the structural measures we use are small or statistically unresolved, and clear suppression of the connected crystalline correlation sets in once ηdis\eta_{\mathrm{dis}} becomes appreciable; no window of disorder-enhanced crystalline coherence is seen within those measures over the sampled range. We stop short of inferring from this a universal impossibility of disorder-stabilized local order: the microscopic result is a statement about the specific disorder models, parameter ranges, and structural diagnostics of this paper, and the Imry–Ma–Larkin theorem below bears on long-range order rather than on finite-domain energetics. The physically relevant parameters for the appearance of a solid-looking density are ηdis\eta_{\mathrm{dis}} and the ratio of the disorder energy to the Coulomb scale e2/ae^{2}/a, and the question with a sharp answer within the present approximations is which of these two energies organizes the electrons. We emphasize in this context that even liquids have strong short-range order on the scale of the interparticle separation aa, and thus short-range order by itself does not imply local solidity; it only implies the existence of a strong repulsive interaction.

Each section considers a slightly different problem and model. The remainder of the paper substantiates this picture through explicit calculation. Section 2 develops the zero-field Hartree–Fock theory of a spin-polarized 2D electron gas with randomly placed Coulomb impurities of both signs, establishes a density-image-level diagnostic of “amorphous solid versus Wigner crystal,” and maps out the (rs,n¯i/n)(r_{s},\bar{n}_{i}/n) structural crossover diagram. Section 3 performs variational Monte Carlo calculations with N=16N=16 spin-polarized electrons at rs=10,20,30,50r_{s}=10,20,30,50 in three disorder models (point-like impurities, impurity-strength scan, and a layer of modulation-type donors), and shows that at no density, in any of the three models, in any of three trial-wave-function families, does charged disorder increase the connected crystalline correlation. Section 4 applies the same programme to the lowest Landau level, in the presence of a strong perpendicular magnetic field, where kinetic energy is quenched and the clean system is already a Wigner crystal: in this case the impurity-driven loss of crystalline coherence is seen in a controlled setting whose dimensionless control parameter is ηdis\eta_{\mathrm{dis}} alone. Section 5 studies the problem of long-range Coulomb disorder at setback dd with nonlinear Thomas–Fermi screening, compares the half-depletion (“percolation”) density of the semiclassical landscape with the Ioffe–Regel–Mott density of Born–RPA transport, and connects the result to the longstanding debate on the 2D metal–insulator transition. Section 6 compares with the independent quantum Hartree–Fock and classical molecular dynamics study of Das Sarma and Pan [30], which identifies the Larkin coherence length with weak-pinning scaling Rc∝W−1R_{c}\propto W^{-1} in the HF amplitude scan and Rc∝n¯i−1/2R_{c}\propto\bar{n}_{i}^{-1/2} in the classical concentration scan, in agreement with the picture built up here. Section 7 discusses the implications for the MoSe2 STM imaging experiments and for the 2D MIT in Si and GaAs, and Sec. 8 summarizes. Much of the work with most of the results presented in Secs. 2–5 is new.

2 Zero-Field Hartree–Fock Theory of a Two-Dimensional Electron Gas with Charged Impurities

We begin with the mean-field (Hartree–Fock) treatment of the simplest version of the problem: a spin-polarized 2D electron gas in a landscape of randomly placed Coulomb impurities of both signs. Hartree–Fock, which neglects correlation, places the clean crystallization at a lower rsr_{s} than the quantum many-body result (a commensurate HF search gives rs≃2.65r_{s}\simeq 2.65 in the fully spin-polarized gas, Sec. 1); this is the virtue of the method here, not its defect, because any disorder-driven enhancement of crystallization would appear most readily within HF. The main HF result below is that no such enhancement is found.

2.1 Model

We consider NN spin-polarized electrons of band mass m∗m^{*} in a medium of dielectric constant ϵ\epsilon, with areal density n=1/[π​(rs​aB∗)2]n=1/[\pi(r_{s}a_{B}^{*})^{2}] and aB∗=ℏ2​ϵ/(m∗​e2)a_{B}^{*}=\hbar^{2}\epsilon/(m^{*}e^{2}). Lengths are measured in units of rs​aB∗r_{s}a_{B}^{*}, 𝐱=𝐫/(rs​aB∗)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{r}/(r_{s}a_{B}^{*}), and energies in the effective Hartree H∗=e2/(ϵ​aB∗)H^{*}=e^{2}/(\epsilon a_{B}^{*}). The Hamiltonian is

H=\displaystyle H={} −12​rs2∑i∇𝐱i2+1rs∑i<j1|𝐱i−𝐱j|\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2r_{s}^{2}}\sum_{i}\nabla_{\mathbf{x}_{i}}^{2}+\frac{1}{r_{s}}\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{x}_{j}|}
−Zrs∑i,αsα|𝐱i−𝐗α|+Hbg.\displaystyle-\frac{Z}{r_{s}}\sum_{i,\alpha}\frac{s_{\alpha}}{|\mathbf{x}_{i}-\mathbf{X}_{\alpha}|}+H_{\rm bg}. (2)

The first term is the kinetic energy, which scales as rs−2r_{s}^{-2}. The second is the electron-electron Coulomb repulsion, which scales as rs−1r_{s}^{-1}. The third couples each electron to quenched point charges sα​Z​es_{\alpha}Ze (sα=±1s_{\alpha}=\pm 1) at random positions 𝐗α\mathbf{X}_{\alpha} in the electron plane through the bare Coulomb interaction. The impurities come in equal numbers of each sign, so their net charge vanishes. HbgH_{\rm bg} is a uniform positive background that neutralizes the electrons and removes the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 components of all Coulomb terms.

The dimensionless parameters are rsr_{s}, ZZ, and ni/nn_{i}/n, where nin_{i} is the total impurity density. We take Z=1Z=1 unless stated otherwise. The electron-impurity and electron-electron terms carry the same prefactor 1/rs1/r_{s}. The ratio of these two bare energy scales is therefore fixed by ZZ and ni/nn_{i}/n alone; the response of the electrons to the impurities still depends on rsr_{s} through the kinetic energy. For short-range disorder of fixed amplitude WW, by contrast, the ratio to the Coulomb scale EC∼H∗/rsE_{C}\sim H^{*}/r_{s} grows as rsr_{s}, or falls as rs−1r_{s}^{-1} if WW is fixed relative to EFE_{F}.

2.2 Method

We solve Eq. (2) in unrestricted HF theory in a periodic triangular supercell containing Nc=16N_{c}=16 electrons, spanning 4×44\times 4 primitive cells of a triangular lattice with spacing a=(2​π/3)1/2​rs​aB∗a=(2\pi/\sqrt{3})^{1/2}r_{s}a_{B}^{*}. Orbitals are expanded in 163 plane waves (|𝐆|≤1.67​G1|\mathbf{G}|\leq 1.67\,G_{1}, with G1=4​π/3​aG_{1}=4\pi/\sqrt{3}a). The Fock matrix contains four terms: the kinetic energy; the Hartree potential 2​π​ρ𝐝/(A​rs​|𝐝|)2\pi\rho_{\mathbf{d}}/(Ar_{s}|\mathbf{d}|), where ρ𝐝\rho_{\mathbf{d}} are the density Fourier coefficients per cell; the exchange potential; and the impurity potential

U𝐝=−2​π​ZA​rs​|𝐝|∑αsαe−i𝐝⋅𝐗α.U_{\mathbf{d}}=-\frac{2\pi Z}{A\,r_{s}|\mathbf{d}|}\sum_{\alpha}s_{\alpha}e^{-i\mathbf{d}\cdot\mathbf{X}_{\alpha}}. (3)

Here AA is the supercell area and 𝐝\mathbf{d} runs over supercell reciprocal vectors. The exchange Coulomb kernel is averaged over each Bloch-mesh cell, with the singular cell integrated exactly. The plane-wave cutoff regularizes the in-plane impurity potential at short distance. Electronic screening of the impurities is generated self-consistently; impurity setback and gate screening are not included. Occupations are Fermi–Dirac at kB​T=0.005​EFk_{B}T=0.005E_{F}, reached by annealing; every state has a density-matrix residual 10−610^{-6}.

For each liquid-side point we start from three seeds: the uniform state, the self-consistent Hartree state, and a lattice-seeded state. For configuration A at rs=4r_{s}=4 the seeds are the clean crystal, the Hartree state, and, where available, the solution at the next lower impurity density. We retain the lowest free energy. Direct-only Hartree with identical impurities isolates exchange. The impurity densities ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8, 1/41/4, 1/21/2, and 1 correspond to 2, 4, 8, and 16 impurities per supercell, drawn as nested subsets of each random configuration. We study five configurations at rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4, labeled A–E, and three at rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0. Configuration A also provides a crystalline comparison at rs=4r_{s}=4.

2.3 Clean reference

The uniform-state energy on a finite Bloch mesh fluctuates with the discrete sampling of the Fermi sea; its error reaches 6×10−4​H∗6\times 10^{-4}H^{*} on a 4×44\times 4 mesh. We therefore compare lattice-seeded solutions with the exact uniform HF energy Eu=rs−2−8/(3​π​rs)E_{u}=r_{s}^{-2}-8/(3\pi r_{s}).

Figure 1(a) shows the comparison. On the 4×44\times 4 mesh the crystal lies EuE_{u} by 3.4×10−43.4\times 10^{-4}, 5.9×10−45.9\times 10^{-4}, and 1.0×10−3​H∗1.0\times 10^{-3}H^{*} at rs=2.7r_{s}=2.7, 2.82.8, and 3.03.0. At rs=2.5r_{s}=2.5 and 2.62.6 the lattice seed yields only a weak modulation (density contrast C≤0.006C\leq 0.006), and at rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 it relaxes to uniform density. These differences are comparable to the remaining mesh error, so we regard rc≃2.65r_{c}\simeq 2.65 as an estimated crossing within this search; our conclusions do not depend on its precise value. It agrees with the boundary rs≈2.7r_{s}\approx 2.7 which the fully polarized unrestricted HF ground state becomes an incommensurate triangular crystal with about 11% more sites than electrons [5]. With spin freedom the commensurate crystal is favored for rs>1.22r_{s}>1.22 [6]. Our commensurate search excludes incommensurate states [7, 5]. The uniform state is our model of the electron liquid, and the results are the response of this reference. We study the liquid side at rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0 and 2.42.4.

The disordered calculations use a 2×22\times 2 mesh. Repeating configuration A at rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 and ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8 on a 4×44\times 4 mesh raises the registered fraction (defined) from 0.63 to 0.94 and the local bond order from 0.52 to 0.61; for this case the coarse mesh understates crystalline order.

2.4 Exchange-enhanced, nonlinear response

To isolate the response mechanism we scale all impurity charges by λ\lambda at fixed positions [Fig. 1(b)]. The Hartree response reproduces the linear response of the uniform reference to within 10% at λ=0.03\lambda=0.03, using an independently computed static susceptibility. The HF response reaches its linear plateau only for λ≲0.003\lambda\lesssim 0.003. On that plateau the total density power at ni/n=1/2n_{i}/n=1/2 exceeds the Hartree value by a factor of 18, which corresponds to an rms amplitude ratio of about 4.2. For the spin-polarized gas 2​kF/G1=(2​3/π)1/2≃1.052k_{F}/G_{1}=(2\sqrt{3}/\pi)^{1/2}\simeq 1.05, so the 2​kF2k_{F} scale of this response lies next to the first reciprocal shell of the Wigner lattice. The corresponding real-space Friedel period is π/kF≃0.825​a\pi/k_{F}\simeq 0.825a.

At λ=1\lambda=1 the HF power per λ2\lambda^{2} has fallen 16-fold its plateau. Impurities with Z=1Z=1 act far outside the linear regime, so the density patterns are nonlinear responses.

2.5 Structural measures

We locate maxima of n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}) exceeding n¯\bar{n}. A maximum within 0.5​a0.5a of a positive impurity is labeled bound; the others are free. For every maximum we compute the charge QjQ_{j} in its Voronoi cell and compare it with the charge e​n¯​Aje\bar{n}A_{j} that the uniform density would place in the same cell. For the free maxima we compute the mean local bond order ⟨|ψ6|⟩\langle|\psi_{6}|\rangle, where |ψ6|=|z−1​∑je6​i​θj||\psi_{6}|=|z^{-1}\sum_{j}e^{6i\theta_{j}}| is taken over the zz Delaunay neighbors. For all maxima we compute the registered fraction: the fraction of pristine lattice sites lying within 0.25​a0.25a of a maximum after optimal translation.

Each state is compared with a null model matched to its selection rules. The bound maxima are kept in place. The free maxima are placed at random subject to the two conditions that hold in the data: they stay at least 0.5​a0.5a from every positive impurity, and they are separated from all other maxima by at least the minimum separation observed among the free maxima of that state. The null configurations pass through the identical triangulation and registration pipeline. We report the percentile of each observed quantity among 300 null samples. A percentile of 100 means that the observed value exceeds every sample, i.e., an estimated tail probability 1/3001/300. Percentiles measure unusualness relative to each state’s own null, not absolute order.

2.6 Density maxima

Figure 2 shows representative densities. On the liquid side, every HF state with impurities contains 14–17 maxima for 16 electrons. The Hartree densities with the same impurities contain 11–21 maxima, with no fixed relation to the electron number. The Voronoi cells of free maxima hold 0.94–0.98 of their uniform-density charge for ni/n≤1/4n_{i}/n\leq 1/4 and 0.78–0.86 at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1. Free maxima therefore redistribute charge within their cells rather than accumulating it. Bound maxima hold 1.2–2.1 times the uniform-density charge. These are features of the density; we do not address orbital localization, and the supercell admits Bloch states.

2.7 Order versus impurity density

Figure 3 gives the percentiles. At rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 the median percentiles of the local bond order and the registered fraction across the five configurations are 97 and 95 at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8; 87 and 92 at 1/41/4; 91 and 95 at 1/21/2; and 32 and 51 at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1. Two configurations at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8 reach a registered fraction of 0.94 with ⟨|ψ6|⟩=0.72\langle|\psi_{6}|\rangle=0.72 and 0.81, exceeding every null sample: crystal-like order across the cell. Results at rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0 are similar. The sixfold-coordinated fraction of free maxima drops from 0.68 at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8 to 0.26 at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1.

The clean crystal at rs=4r_{s}=4 with configuration A sits at the 100th percentile in both measures for ni/n≤1/4n_{i}/n\leq 1/4. It falls to the 22nd and 32nd percentiles at ni/n=1/2n_{i}/n=1/2 and lies at the 85th and 50th at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1. At ni/n=1/2n_{i}/n=1/2 the liquid-side states thus remain in the upper tail of their nulls while this crystal-side state does not.

2.8 Origin of the dilute-limit order

In a 16-electron periodic cell, the impurities at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8 are a single ±\pm pair repeated with period 4​a4a, an arrangement commensurate with the triangular lattice. The Hartree control at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8 has registered-fraction percentiles 15–85 with median 81: elevated, but the HF median of 95. This is consistent with a commensurate imprint that exists without exchange and that exchange strengthens, both through the enhanced response and by organizing the density into maxima close in number to the electrons. A 36-electron supercell separates the two contributions. There the local bond order of free maxima exceeds at least 98% of the matched null samples for ni/n≤2/9n_{i}/n\leq 2/9 in every configuration and falls into the null range at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1, while the cell-wide registered fraction stays at 0.3–0.5. The local order is robust; the cell-wide registry of the smaller cell includes a commensurate contribution.

2.9 Short-range disorder

We provide in the calculated results for HF theory in the presence of short-range Gaussian random disorder of rms strength WW, computed in the same cell and tested against the same null model. There the disorder does not produce apparent local crystalline order, in contrast to the Coulomb case: on the liquid side the median bond-order percentile stays between 34 and 87 for W/EF=0.5W/E_{F}=0.5–10. It drives both the Wigner crystal (large rsr_{s}) and the liquid (small rsr_{s}) into the amorphous-solid regime through disorder-induced crossovers. The local crystalline order found here is thus tied to dilute charged impurities.

2.10 Strong disorder

As ni/nn_{i}/n increases, attractive centers acquire maxima, repulsive centers expel density, and random ±\pm charges generate long-wavelength potential variations (v⁡(q)∝1/qv(q)\propto 1/q). At ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1 the typical order of liquid-side states falls toward the null level, with substantial configuration dependence, and the density becomes an amorphous pattern that follows the impurity configuration. Section 2.12 collects the 16-electron results in a diagram in the rsr_{s}–ni/nn_{i}/n plane.

2.11 Structural observables relevant to STM imaging

Within the specific HF model and parameter range reported above, three structural observations connect to the experimental literature on disordered 2D electron solids imaged by scanning tunneling microscopy [12, 13]; we present them as structural signatures of the amorphous-solid picture, leaving comparison with the published image analyses to the experimental literature.

(i) Density maxima at the interelectron spacing arise from a uniform reference state under charged disorder at every impurity density studied. Such maxima alone do not discriminate between a liquid response, a pinned crystal, and an impurity-templated state. Crystalline information resides in order beyond nearest neighbors, tested against a matched null model and compared with the mapped defect positions.

(ii) Charged impurities up to ni/n=1/2n_{i}/n=1/2 produce density patterns that are typically more ordered than the matched null in a state that is uniform when clean. In the 16-electron cell some configurations reach crystal-like registry across the cell; in the 36-electron cell the enhanced order is local. This order depends on the impurity configuration and likely includes a contribution from the commensurate periodic cell. Short-range disorder produces nonperiodic density puddles instead, so the two defect populations characterized separately in Ref. [13] are expected to affect density images differently. The experimental defect arrangement is neither periodic nor commensurate. Its effect on the extent of such order is a separate question that our calculation does not settle.

(iii) The amorphous regime at ni/n≃1n_{i}/n\simeq 1 is the structural counterpart of the strong-disorder picture of Babbar et al. [20], in which the low-density solid is controlled by the random impurity potential rather than by a clean crystalline order parameter. Their identification rests on transport, which we do not compute. Random charged impurities, modeled here, are the dominant scatterers in doped 2D semiconductors [34, 35]. A quantitative comparison with Ref. [13] (rs≈18r_{s}\approx 18) requires the defect density per carrier, impurity setback, and gate screening.

2.12 Diagram in the rsr_{s}–ni/nn_{i}/n plane

Data.—The diagram uses the 16-electron supercell (4×44\times 4 triangular), 163 plane waves, a 2×22\times 2 Bloch mesh, and kB​T=0.005​EFk_{B}T=0.005E_{F}, with charged impurities of valence Z=1Z=1 in equal numbers of each sign. All points use one nested impurity configuration (configuration A of the preceding subsection). The grid is rs=2.0, 2.4, 3, 4, 8, 16r_{s}=2.0,\,2.4,\,3,\,4,\,8,\,16 and ni/n=0, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1, 2, 10n_{i}/n=0,\,1/8,\,1/4,\,1/2,\,1,\,2,\,10, i.e., 0, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and 160 impurities per supercell. For each point, HF solutions are started from the clean state (uniform for rs<rcr_{s}<r_{c}, crystalline otherwise), the Hartree state with the same impurities, and, where available, a third seed: the solution at the next lower impurity density, or a lattice-seeded state for rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 and for rs=8r_{s}=8 and 16 at ni/n≤1/4n_{i}/n\leq 1/4. The lowest free energy is retained. All states satisfy a density-matrix residual below 10−610^{-6}, except rs=16r_{s}=16 at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8, which is not fully converged.

Measures.—Two quantities classify each state. (i) The first-shell coherence length ξB\xi_{B} is the first e−1e^{-1} crossing of the demodulated first-shell density correlation, evaluated on the density clipped at 2​n¯2\bar{n}. The clipping removes the peak height of maxima at attractive centers, which is set by the short-distance regularization. In this cell ξB\xi_{B} is bounded above by half the cell side, 2​a2a, and below by the value 0.64​a0.64a produced by a featureless spectrum. (ii) The bound fraction fbf_{b} is the fraction of density maxima lying within 0.5​a0.5a of an attractive impurity.

Classification.—A state is labeled WS if ξB>a\xi_{B}>a, i.e., if first-shell density-wave coherence extends beyond one pristine lattice spacing within the cell. It is labeled AS (amorphous solid) if ξB≤a\xi_{B}\leq a and fb≥0.4f_{b}\geq 0.4, i.e., if the density is organized around the impurities, with a large fraction of maxima at attractive centers. States with ξB≤a\xi_{B}\leq a and fb<0.4f_{b}<0.4 are labeled FL for rs<rcr_{s}<r_{c}, where the clean reference is uniform and the density is the static response of the liquid. The same states are labeled crossover for rs>rcr_{s}>r_{c}. The labels refer to structural regimes in a finite cell with quenched disorder; they do not identify thermodynamic phases or broken symmetries. With random pinning no state has long-range crystalline order, and “WS” denotes coherence exceeding the accessible range of the cell. The two thresholds separate the data cleanly: ξB\xi_{B} is either ≤0.81​a\leq 0.81a or ≥1.31​a\geq 1.31a, and fbf_{b} is either ≤0.38\leq 0.38 or ≥0.50\geq 0.50.

Features.—Four regimes appear. For rs<rcr_{s}<r_{c} and ni/n≤1/2n_{i}/n\leq 1/2 the density is the static response of the uniform reference (FL): it is strongly modulated and locally ordered (Fig. 3), but first-shell coherence does not extend beyond one lattice spacing and few maxima sit on impurities. For ni/n≥1n_{i}/n\geq 1 the density is organized by the impurities (AS) at every rsr_{s} studied, whether the clean reference is uniform or crystalline: half or more of the maxima sit on attractive centers and coherence is at the resolution floor. Coherence beyond the lattice spacing (WS) occupies the clean crystal and the dilute-impurity region above rcr_{c}, and this region widens with rsr_{s}: at rs=3r_{s}=3 it is limited to the clean system, and at rs=8r_{s}=8 and 16 it extends to ni/n=1/4n_{i}/n=1/4. Between WS and AS on the crystal side lies a crossover region in which first-shell coherence is lost while fewer than 40% of the maxima are bound to impurities. The layout parallels the regimes discussed in Ref. [20]: a weak-disorder crystalline regime at large rsr_{s}, a disorder-dominated regime at large impurity density, and a liquid at weak interaction and weak disorder.

2.13 36-electron supercell

Setup.—The supercell spans 6×66\times 6 primitive cells and contains Nc=36N_{c}=36 electrons. The plane-wave cutoff is the same as in the preceding subsection (|𝐆|≤1.67​G1|\mathbf{G}|\leq 1.67G_{1}, 367 plane waves). We sample the Brillouin zone at Γ\Gamma only, which for this cell gives a kk-point density comparable to the 2×22\times 2 mesh of the 16-electron cell. With this sampling the clean lattice-seeded state relaxes to uniform density at rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0 and 2.22.2 (C<10−4C<10^{-4}). At rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 it keeps a weak commensurate modulation (C=0.003C=0.003). Impurity configurations in this cell are drawn independently of those in the 16-electron cell and are labeled A′–C′. The liquid-side calculations use rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0 (configuration A′) and rs=2.2r_{s}=2.2 (configurations A′–C′). The clean crystal at rs=4r_{s}=4 (configuration A′) serves as the crystalline reference. Integer, charge-neutral impurity numbers give ni/n=1/9n_{i}/n=1/9, 2/92/9, 1/21/2, and 1 (4, 8, 18, and 36 impurities). Seeds, selection by free energy, and the matched null model (bound maxima fixed; free maxima at least 0.5​a0.5a from attractive impurities and separated by the observed minimum spacing) are as in the preceding subsection. HF states are compared with 200 null samples, Hartree states with 100, and the rs=4r_{s}=4 states with 150.

Results.—The 36-electron calculations reproduce the trends of the 16-electron cell (Figs. 5, 6; Table 2). On the liquid side the HF density contains 31–41 maxima for 36 electrons. At dilute impurity density (ni/n=1/9n_{i}/n=1/9 and 2/92/9) the local bond order of free maxima exceeds at least 98% of the matched null samples in every configuration, with ⟨|ψ6|⟩=0.42\langle|\psi_{6}|\rangle=0.42–0.520.52. It decreases at ni/n=1/2n_{i}/n=1/2 (percentiles 79–100) and falls into the null range at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1 (percentiles 6.5–81.5), where 16–19 of the maxima sit on attractive centers. The rs=4r_{s}=4 crystal shows the same approach to the null at ni/n≥1/2n_{i}/n\geq 1/2. The Hartree densities with the same impurities contain 31–38 maxima. Their mean local bond order at ni/n=1/9n_{i}/n=1/9 and 2/92/9 is 0.41, against 0.48 for HF, and their bond-order percentiles span 41–100.

Two features differ from the 16-electron cell. The registered fraction at dilute impurity density is 0.31–0.50, whereas two 16-electron configurations reached 0.94; its percentiles range from 43.5 to 99.5. Cell-wide registry is therefore weaker in the larger cell, while local order persists. This indicates a commensurate contribution to the cell-wide registry of the 16-electron cell, where the impurities at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8 form a single ±\pm pair repeated with period 4​a4a. The Voronoi charge of free maxima is 0.95–0.98 of the uniform-density charge of the same cell at dilute impurity density and 0.82–0.89 at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1, as in the 16-electron cell: free maxima redistribute charge within their cells, and charge accumulates at attractive centers.

Additional 16-electron data.—At rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0 (three configurations) the median percentiles of local bond order and registered fraction in the 16-electron cell are 91 and 84 at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8, 72 and 49 at 1/41/4, 92 and 90 at 1/21/2, and 36 and 39 at ni/n=1n_{i}/n=1, following the rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 trend of the preceding subsection.

2.14 Short-range Gaussian disorder

Model and method.—We replace the charged-impurity term of Eq. (2) by a Gaussian white-noise potential V⁡(𝐫)V(\mathbf{r}). It is generated on a 32×3232\times 32 grid spanning the supercell (grid spacing a/8a/8) from independent unit-normal variables, with the mean removed and the rms normalized to WW, and it enters the Fock matrix through its Fourier coefficients on the supercell reciprocal vectors of the basis. The potential is zero-range on the scale of the lattice spacing, with the grid spacing as its short-distance cutoff. All other elements are those of the charged-impurity calculations: the 16-electron cell, 163 plane waves, the 2×22\times 2 Bloch mesh, kB​T=0.005​EFk_{B}T=0.005E_{F}, three seeds (the clean state, the Hartree state with the same potential, and a lattice-seeded state), and selection by free energy. We use W/EF=0.5W/E_{F}=0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10, with three disorder realizations at rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 and one at rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0 and rs=4r_{s}=4. All states satisfy a density-matrix residual below 10−610^{-6}. Because WW is fixed in units of EFE_{F}, its ratio to the Coulomb scale falls as rs−1r_{s}^{-1}, unlike the charged-impurity case, where the ratio of bare energy scales is independent of rsr_{s}. The structural measures and the matched null model are those of the preceding subsection; with no discrete impurity centers, all density maxima are free, and the null model randomizes all of them subject to the observed minimum separation (300 samples).

Results.—On the liquid side (Figs. 7 and 8), short-range disorder turns the uniform density into an increasingly inhomogeneous, nonperiodic landscape of density puddles: the density contrast at rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 grows from C=0.02C=0.02–0.05 at W/EF=0.5W/E_{F}=0.5 to 2.7–3.0 at W/EF=10W/E_{F}=10. The median percentile of the local bond order stays within the matched-null range at every disorder strength; individual realizations lie between the 2nd and 99th percentiles without a systematic trend. The median over the three realizations at rs=2.4r_{s}=2.4 is 79, 66, 66, 87, and 34 for W/EF=0.5W/E_{F}=0.5, 1, 2, 5, and 10, and the values at rs=2.0r_{s}=2.0 are 80, 95, 73, 87, and 67. The coherence length stays at 0.61–0.85aa, and the registered fraction falls from percentiles 54–100 at W/EF=0.5W/E_{F}=0.5 to 4–13 at W/EF=10W/E_{F}=10, below the null: the density is increasingly selected by the disorder rather than by lattice registry. The Hartree control with the same potential gives bond-order percentiles 64–99, comparable to HF: exchange does not enhance local order for this disorder.

On the crystal side (rs=4r_{s}=4) weak disorder preserves the crystal: at W/EF=0.5W/E_{F}=0.5 the coherence length exceeds the 2​a2a ceiling and every lattice site is registered. At W/EF=1W/E_{F}=1 the coherence length is 1.01​a1.01a, at W/EF=2W/E_{F}=2 it falls to 0.76​a0.76a, and at W/EF=5W/E_{F}=5 and 10 it is 0.67​a0.67a, equal to the liquid-side values. The registered-fraction percentile drops from 100 to 20–35 over the same range, and at W/EF=10W/E_{F}=10 the density contrast (C=2.8C=2.8) matches the liquid side. Increasing short-range disorder thus drives both the Wigner crystal at large rsr_{s} and the Fermi liquid at small rsr_{s} into a common disorder-selected amorphous-solid (AS) regime through disorder-induced crossovers; for rs=4r_{s}=4 the crossover lies near W/EF≃1W/E_{F}\simeq 1–2. These are structural crossovers, not thermodynamic phase transitions.

Comparison with charged impurities.—The two disorder types agree at strong disorder: in both, liquid-side and crystal-side states converge to an amorphous density selected by the disorder. They differ on the liquid side at weak disorder. Dilute charged impurities produce local bond order above the matched null: median percentile 97 at ni/n=1/8n_{i}/n=1/8 in the 16-electron cell (Fig. 3) and at least 98 in every 36-electron configuration at ni/n≤2/9n_{i}/n\leq 2/9 (Sec. 2.13). Short-range Gaussian disorder, analyzed identically, produces no systematic local order beyond the null at any strength. A plausible reason is that a dilute set of Coulomb centers acts at discrete points and leaves impurity-free regions, where the exchange-enhanced response of the liquid, peaked near 2​kF≃G12k_{F}\simeq G_{1}, organizes the density locally, whereas a zero-range Gaussian potential acts everywhere, with no preferred wave vector, and imposes its own nonperiodic pattern. In these calculations, apparent local crystalline order in the density of a liquid arises with dilute charged disorder and not with short-range disorder.

3 Variational Monte Carlo of the 2D Electron System with Charged Impurities

The Hartree–Fock analysis of Sec. 2 is a mean-field calculation. To test whether its conclusions survive at the fully correlated many-body level, we turn to variational Monte Carlo (VMC) with Jastrow–Slater trial wave functions [36], in which the quantum crystallization density of the clean 2D electron gas is in the range of a few tens and depends on the spin sector: Drummond and Needs [3] report the paramagnetic-to-antiferromagnetic-crystal transition at rc=31​(1)r_{c}=31(1), with the ferromagnetic crystal becoming stable at a different density; the fully spin-polarized gas studied here enters the Wigner regime in the same general range. The HF estimate rcHF≃2.65r_{c}^{\mathrm{HF}}\simeq 2.65 lies well below the VMC/DMC estimate; a disorder effect that is visible in HF below rcHFr_{c}^{\mathrm{HF}} should also be visible in VMC below the VMC rcr_{c} if the mechanism is real.

3.1 Models, trial wave functions, diagnostics, and energy scales

3.1.1 Hamiltonian

We consider N=16N=16 fully spin-polarized electrons in a rhombic periodic cell that accommodates a 4×44\times 4 triangular lattice of spacing a=1.90463​rs​aB∗a=1.90463\,r_{s}a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, interacting through the 2D Coulomb interaction with a neutralizing background, in the presence of NiN_{i} quenched point charges ZIZ_{I} (in units of ee) located in a plane a distance dd from the electron plane at positions 𝐑I\mathbf{R}_{I}. In effective atomic units (aB∗=ℏ2​κ/m​e2a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}=\hbar^{2}\kappa/me^{2}, Ha∗=e2/κ​aB∗\mathrm{Ha}^{*}=e^{2}/\kappa a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}),

H=−12∑i∇i2+∑i<j1|𝐫i−𝐫j|−∑i,IZI|𝐫i−𝐑I|2+d2+Ebg,\begin{split}H={}&-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}\nabla_{i}^{2}+\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{r}_{j}|}\\ &-\sum_{i,I}\frac{Z_{I}}{\sqrt{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{2}+d^{2}}}+E_{\rm bg},\end{split} (4)

with all periodic images included through 2D Ewald sums for both the electron–electron and the electron–impurity terms, and EbgE_{\rm bg} the background terms, which are constants. The impurities are frozen; there is no disorder averaging, and each realization is a distinct Hamiltonian whose ground state is calculated separately. This is the appropriate description of an STM experiment, which images one realization.

Three disorder models are studied, each at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, and 50.

  1. (i)

    Strong point-like disorder: Ni=8N_{i}=8 or 1616, half with ZI=+1Z_{I}=+1 and half with ZI=−1Z_{I}=-1 (a neutral set), at d=aB∗d=a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, for two independent random realizations A and B of the positions, with the 8-impurity set nested in the 16-impurity set. The same fractional positions are used at every density (Fig. 9), so that the impurity spacing scales with the electron spacing and n/nin/n_{i} is fixed at 22 (Ni=8N_{i}=8) or 11 (Ni=16N_{i}=16).

  2. (ii)

    Impurity-strength scan: the 16-impurity landscape A (and B as a check at rs=20r_{s}=20) with ZI=±ZZ_{I}=\pm Z, Z=1/50Z=1/50, 1/201/20, 1/101/10, 1/51/5, and 11, at d=aB∗d=a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}.

  3. (iii)

    Donor layer: Ni=16N_{i}=16 impurities of charge ZI=+1Z_{I}=+1 at the 16 positions of landscape A, i.e., a neutral electron–donor system with n/ni=1n/n_{i}=1 as in a modulation-doped structure, at setbacks d=1d=1, 5, 10, and 20​aB∗20\,a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}.

Model (i) is the strong-coupling limit in which each attractive impurity is a hydrogenic trap; model (ii) connects that limit continuously to the clean liquid; model (iii) spans, through the setback, the range from point-like traps to the smooth long-range potential fluctuations in which puddles rather than traps are the natural objects. Models (i) and (ii) coincide at Z=1Z=1; models (ii) and (iii) have the same impurity positions.

3.1.2 Energy and length scales

Three energies compete: the Fermi energy of the polarized gas EF=2/rs2E_{F}=2/r_{s}^{2} (0.0200.020, 0.00500.0050, 0.00220.0022, 0.0008​Ha∗0.0008\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, 50), the nearest-neighbor Coulomb energy e2/a=0.525/rse^{2}/a=0.525/r_{s} (0.05250.0525, 0.02630.0263, 0.01750.0175, 0.0105​Ha∗0.0105\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}), and the impurity binding energy. For a point charge ZZ at setback d≲aB∗d\lesssim a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} the 2D hydrogenic binding energy is of order 2​Z2​Ha∗2Z^{2}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} with orbit radius aB∗/2​Za_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}/2Z; for Z=1Z=1 at d=aB∗d=a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} the VMC gives a bound orbit of rms radius 1.51.5–1.8​aB∗1.8a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, i.e., a binding energy of order 0.5​Ha∗0.5\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}, ten to fifty times e2/ae^{2}/a. This is the trapping regime: whatever the electrons do collectively, an attractive impurity captures one of them. For Z=1/50Z=1/50 the binding energy is ∼10−3​Ha∗\sim 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} and the orbit radius ∼25​aB∗\sim 25a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, comparable to aa; this is the perturbative regime. The crossover, where 2​Z2∼e2/a2Z^{2}\sim e^{2}/a, is at Z≈0.1Z\approx 0.1–0.20.2 for rs=20r_{s}=20–3030, and that is where the physics of model (ii) changes.

For the donor layer the relevant comparison is different. A single donor at setback d≫aB∗d\gg a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} binds classically, with well depth e2/de^{2}/d (0.20.2, 0.10.1, 0.05​Ha∗0.05\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} at d=5d=5, 10, 20​aB∗20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}) and harmonic localization length ℓ=(d3​aB∗)1/4\ell=(d^{3}a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*})^{1/4} (3.33.3, 5.65.6, 9.5​aB∗9.5a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}). Both are again large against e2/ae^{2}/a at every rsr_{s} studied, so the setback alone never switches off single-donor trapping. What decides whether the landscape consists of individual traps or of smooth puddles is the ratio d/ad/a of the setback to the donor spacing (which equals the electron spacing, ni=nn_{i}=n): for d≳a/2d\gtrsim a/2 neighboring donor potentials overlap into a smooth landscape whose corrugation is of order e2/ae^{2}/a, while for d≪ad\ll a each donor is its own trap. At fixed d=10​aB∗d=10a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, d/a=0.53d/a=0.53, 0.260.26, 0.180.18, 0.110.11 at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, 50; at d=20​aB∗d=20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} the same numbers are doubled and at d=5​aB∗d=5a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} halved; at d=aB∗d=a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} every donor is a point trap at every density. Lowering the density at fixed disorder therefore takes the system from the smooth-potential regime to the trapping regime, which is the physical situation in a gate-tunable device, and raising the setback at fixed density does the reverse.

These numbers are the content of the paper in compressed form. At rs<rcr_{s}<r_{c} the electrons are a liquid, and whether they look solid in a density image is decided by the ratio of the disorder energy to e2/ae^{2}/a and by the ratio of the disorder length to aa, not by rsr_{s}.

3.1.3 Trial wave functions

We use conventional Slater–Jastrow VMC [36]. Three trial families are optimized independently for every Hamiltonian:

ΨPW\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm PW} =det[ei​𝐤m⋅𝐫j]​e−U⁡({𝐫})​eW⁡({𝐫}),\displaystyle=\det[e^{i\mathbf{k}_{m}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}}]\,e^{-U(\{\mathbf{r}\})}\,e^{W(\{\mathbf{r}\})}, (5)
ΨPG\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm PG} =det[ϕβ​(𝐫j−𝐬m)]​e−U​eW,𝐬m​on the lattice,\displaystyle=\det[\phi_{\beta}(\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{s}_{m})]\,e^{-U}\,e^{W},\quad\mathbf{s}_{m}\ \text{on the lattice}, (6)
ΨFG\displaystyle\Psi_{\rm FG} =det[ϕβ​(𝐫j−𝐜m)]​e−U​eW,𝐜m​relaxed,\displaystyle=\det[\phi_{\beta}(\mathbf{r}_{j}-\mathbf{c}_{m})]\,e^{-U}\,e^{W},\quad\mathbf{c}_{m}\ \text{relaxed}, (7)

where the plane-wave (PW) determinant uses the 16 lowest closed-shell momenta of the cell, ϕβ\phi_{\beta} is a periodized Gaussian of optimized width β−1/2\beta^{-1/2}, UU is a two-body Jastrow factor of the standard Padé form with an optimized parameter, and W=ℓ∑i,IκIsgn(ZI)exp[−(|𝐫i−𝐑I|2+d2−d)/ℓ]W=\ell\sum_{i,I}\kappa_{I}\,\mathrm{sgn}(Z_{I})\exp[-(\sqrt{|\mathbf{r}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{I}|^{2}+d^{2}}-d)/\ell] is a one-body impurity factor with independently optimized amplitudes κ±\kappa_{\pm} and range ℓ\ell, which lets electrons bind to attractive impurities and avoid repulsive ones. In the pinned-Gaussian family (PG) the orbital centers 𝐬m\mathbf{s}_{m} are the sites of the pristine triangular lattice; in the free-center family (FG) the centers 𝐜m\mathbf{c}_{m} are obtained by relaxing 16 classical point charges in the electron–electron Ewald potential plus the impurity potential smeared over the Gaussian orbital, starting from the lattice and from random positions and keeping the lowest-energy arrangement. The FG family exists precisely so that the calculation can find a disorder-adapted crystalline arrangement if one is energetically preferred: a locally crystalline state whose electrons sit at positions selected by the disorder is representable in FG but not in PW or PG. For the clean system PW and PG are used. All parameters are optimized by stochastic reconfiguration for every Hamiltonian; production runs use 24 Markov chains and 1200 blocks (28 800 stored configurations per state), with errors from chain-to-chain and reblocked statistics. The lowest-energy family is used for the figures; all families are reported in the tables, where the lowest-energy one is marked with an asterisk. Computational details are in Appendix A.

VMC with these trial functions is not exact, and we do not claim quantitative accuracy for energies. The structural conclusions reported below are comparisons between the clean and disordered states of the same model in the same trial family, carried out in whichever families are physically applicable for each disorder model (both PW and PG for Model (i) at Z=1Z=1; all three families for Model (ii)’s charge scan where free-center optimization is defined; FG for the donor layer). Within these subsets the structural inferences are consistent across the families compared, and that consistency, rather than any exact-ground-state claim, is the ground of the discussion that follows.

3.1.4 Diagnostics: what a density image measures and what a crystal requires

The structure factor S⁡(𝐪)=⟨|ρ𝐪|2⟩/NS(\mathbf{q})=\langle|\rho_{\mathbf{q}}|^{2}\rangle/N, ρ𝐪=∑jei​𝐪⋅𝐫j\rho_{\mathbf{q}}=\sum_{j}e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}_{j}}, evaluated at the reciprocal vectors of the periodic cell, decomposes exactly as

S⁡(𝐪)=|⟨ρ𝐪⟩|2N⏟Sst​(𝐪)+⟨|ρ𝐪|2⟩−|⟨ρ𝐪⟩|2N⏟Sc​(𝐪).S(\mathbf{q})=\underbrace{\frac{|\langle\rho_{\mathbf{q}}\rangle|^{2}}{N}}_{S_{\mathrm{st}}(\mathbf{q})}+\underbrace{\frac{\langle|\rho_{\mathbf{q}}|^{2}\rangle-|\langle\rho_{\mathbf{q}}\rangle|^{2}}{N}}_{S_{c}(\mathbf{q})}. (8)

The static part SstS_{\mathrm{st}} is the Fourier power of the one-body density n⁡(𝐫)=⟨∑jδ⁡(𝐫−𝐫j)⟩n(\mathbf{r})=\langle\sum_{j}\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}_{j})\rangle; it is nonzero only when something external (here the impurities, or the trial lattice in PG/FG) selects positions. A time-averaged density image, which is what STM records in the simplest limit (Sec. 3.5), measures n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}) and hence SstS_{\mathrm{st}} and nothing else. The connected part ScS_{c} measures the correlation of density fluctuations; a clean crystal of NN electrons in a periodic cell, which has uniform n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}) because nothing selects its position, has all of its crystalline signal in ScS_{c}, and a crystal pinned by disorder keeps its crystalline correlations in ScS_{c} while acquiring a static part. The central point of this paper is that disorder moves weight from ScS_{c} to SstS_{\mathrm{st}}. We quote SS, SstS_{\mathrm{st}}, and ScS_{c} at the first star of reciprocal vectors {𝐆1}\{\mathbf{G}_{1}\} of the pristine triangular lattice, which is the crystal wave vector and also where the liquid’s S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) peaks, and we show full maps; we also record the maximum of Sc​(𝐪)S_{c}(\mathbf{q}) over all wave vectors, which would detect a crystal of any orientation.

Real-space order is quantified by the pair correlation g⁡(r)g(r) and by the sixfold bond-orientational order ψ6,i=16​∑j∈𝒩6​(i)e6​i​θi​j\psi_{6,i}=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_{6}(i)}e^{6i\theta_{ij}} over the six nearest neighbors of electron ii; we report the local amplitude ⟨|ψ6,i|⟩\langle|\psi_{6,i}|\rangle and the global amplitude ⟨|1N​∑iψ6,i|⟩\langle|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\psi_{6,i}|\rangle, and for model (i) also the local amplitude of the unbound electrons alone, with the impurity-bound electrons removed from the neighbor lists. The clean liquid at rs=10r_{s}=10–20 has ⟨|ψ6|⟩≃0.37\langle|\psi_{6}|\rangle\simeq 0.37–0.380.38 and the clean rs=50r_{s}=50 crystal has 0.430.43; the local amplitude is far from zero in the liquid because nearest-neighbor shells are always roughly sixfold at these densities. This is the quantitative form of the statement that every correlated liquid has crystalline coherence on the scale of aa. Pinning is quantified by the mean number of electrons within a given distance of an attractive impurity, compared with the value that a uniform density would give (for eight attractive impurities, 72/rs272/r_{s}^{2} within 3​aB∗3a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} and 1.81.8 within a/4a/4). For the donor layer we also report the fraction of the cell with n⁡(𝐫)>n¯/2n(\mathbf{r})>\bar{n}/2 and whether that region, or its complement, spans the periodic cell; on N=16N=16 this is a statement about morphology, not a percolation calculation.

3.1.5 What ScS_{c} measures and what it does not

A caveat to Eq. (8) deserves to be stated plainly, because it bears on how the tables below should be read. The connected structure factor Sc​(𝐪)S_{c}(\mathbf{q}) measures the correlation of fluctuations of ρ𝐪\rho_{\mathbf{q}} about its mean, not positional order as such. Positional order can reside wholly, or partly, or not at all in ScS_{c} depending on the trial state and the ensemble averaging. A trial wave function whose electrons are tied to definite lattice sites, as in the lattice-Gaussian (PG) family, places the Bragg weight in SstS_{\mathrm{st}} and leaves ScS_{c} to measure the residual fluctuations about the lattice; a trial wave function whose density is translation-invariant, as in the plane-wave (PW) family, places all crystalline signal that is there in ScS_{c} and has Sst=0S_{\mathrm{st}}=0 identically. The paper’s own clean benchmarks at rs=50r_{s}=50 in Table 3 illustrate this: the clean PG state has (S,Sst,Sc)≃(3.46,2.28,1.18)(S,S_{\mathrm{st}},S_{c})\simeq(3.46,2.28,1.18), while the clean PW trial has Sc≃1.66S_{c}\simeq 1.66, so a ranking by ScS_{c} alone would favor the delocalized PW reference over the lattice-pinned PG trial that is at lower energy and is the physical reference crystal at this density. The lesson is that ScS_{c} is not an orientation-independent crystallinity measure, and a decrease in ScS_{c} does not by itself establish the loss of positional order. We therefore quote SS and SstS_{\mathrm{st}} alongside ScS_{c}, and rely on real-space diagnostics – the sixfold bond amplitude ⟨|ψ6|⟩\langle|\psi_{6}|\rangle, the impurity-registered fraction of density maxima, the pair correlation g⁡(r)g(r), and the first-shell density coherence length – as the primary structural inferences in the discussion below. ScS_{c} enters as a fluctuation diagnostic that complements these, not as a standalone crystallinity measure.

3.1.6 Definitions

To keep the terminology fixed: a Wigner crystal (WC) is interaction-driven periodic order of the electron density, with Bragg peaks; it exists only in the clean limit and is characterized by positional order that is coherent across the sample (reflected in S⁡(𝐆)∝NS(\mathbf{G})\propto N, with the weight distributed between SstS_{\mathrm{st}} and ScS_{c} according to the ensemble convention). A pinned Wigner crystal is a WC whose translational coherence has been cut off by disorder at a length ξ≫a\xi\gg a with a density of defects that is small inside domains; it retains crystalline correlations over many shells. An amorphous solid (AS) is a state with a static, inhomogeneous density whose peaks are organized by the disorder, with crystalline correlations extending at most to the nearest-neighbor shell. “Wigner solid” (WS) is a term in common use in the imaging-experiment literature; in the HF classification of Sec. 2 it was used as a finite-cell structural label for states with first-shell density-wave coherence extending beyond one lattice spacing in the cell, and the same shorthand is used here, with the operational structural meaning carried by the WC/pinned-WC/AS distinction above. Part of the purpose of the structural diagnostics introduced here is to tell, within the present approximations, which of the above pictures a given calculated state resembles.

3.2 Strong point-like disorder at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, 50

Figures 10–12 and Table 3 contain the results for model (i): unit charges of both signs one Bohr radius from the plane, at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, and 50, for two impurity densities and two realizations. The physics is the same in all sixteen disordered Hamiltonians and is dictated by the energy scales of Sec. 3.1.2.

Each attractive impurity captures one electron, independent of rsr_{s}. The number of electrons within 3​aB∗3a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} of an attractive impurity is 3.43.4–3.53.5 for four attractive impurities and 6.46.4–7.07.0 for eight, i.e., 0.800.80–0.880.88 per impurity, at all four densities alike (Table 3); the probability of double occupancy is below 10% at rs=10r_{s}=10 and below 3% at rs≥30r_{s}\geq 30. Figure 13 shows the radial density of the bound electron around its impurity on the aB∗a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} scale: it is the same hydrogenic orbit, of rms radius 1.51.5–1.8​aB∗1.8a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, and 50, because the binding energy (∼0.5​Ha∗\sim 0.5\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}) is one to two orders of magnitude larger than every interaction scale. The bright spots in Fig. 10 are these orbits, and they are the same spots at rs=10r_{s}=10 and at rs=50r_{s}=50. Their size is aB∗a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, ten to fifty times smaller than aa; a density image of this state shows an array of resolved “electrons” whose number is Ni/2N_{i}/2 and whose positions are {𝐑I:ZI>0}\{\mathbf{R}_{I}:Z_{I}>0\}, with no reference to the electron density nn at all.

The remaining electrons are the clean system at a lower density in a landscape of holes. The N−Ni/2N-N_{i}/2 unbound electrons (12.512.5 or 99) see the bare repulsive impurities, each of which carves a hole of radius ∼a\sim a (the potential 1/r2+d21/\sqrt{r^{2}+d^{2}} equals e2/ae^{2}/a at r≃ar\simeq a), and the neutral impurity–electron complexes, whose residual field is dipolar and weak. At rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, and 30 these electrons remain a liquid: the density between the holes is smooth, with no resolvable maxima (Fig. 10), their local bond order ⟨|ψ6|⟩m\langle|\psi_{6}|\rangle_{\rm m} (0.350.35–0.370.37) is at or below the clean value of the lowest-energy clean state (0.370.37, 0.380.38, 0.400.40 at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30), and the spread of their nearest-neighbor distances is wider than in the clean liquid. Nothing in the unbound population is more crystalline than the clean liquid; the only new static structure is the impurity-bound spots and the holes.

The connected crystalline correlation is suppressed at every rsr_{s}. Sc​(𝐆1)S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1}) falls from 1.11.1–1.21.2 (clean, lowest-energy family, rs=10r_{s}=10–30) to 0.720.72–0.830.83 with 8 impurities and 0.450.45–0.590.59 with 16; the static part grows from 00 (PW) or 0.10.1–1.01.0 (PG, trial-lattice imprint) to 0.30.3–1.31.3. The full S⁡(𝐪)S(\mathbf{q}) maps of the disordered states (Fig. 11) contain many sharp features, and all of them are static: they are the autocorrelation of the impurity positions. Subtracting the static part (Fig. 12) leaves a structureless connected map with less weight at the crystal wave vector than the clean liquid has. At rs=30r_{s}=30, where the clean lattice-Gaussian state is already the lower-energy clean state and carries an incipient-crystal star (Sst=0.98S_{\mathrm{st}}=0.98, Sc=1.21S_{c}=1.21), the same impurities reduce the connected star to 0.760.76–0.830.83 (8 impurities) and 0.500.50–0.560.56 (16 impurities), the same values as at rs=10r_{s}=10 and 20 within the realization-to-realization spread.

At rs=50r_{s}=50 the same impurities destroy the crystal. The clean PG crystal has S⁡(𝐆1)=3.5S(\mathbf{G}_{1})=3.5, of which 2.32.3 is static (the pinned position of the finite crystal in the trial function) and 1.21.2 connected; the clean PW liquid-like trial, which cannot pin, has Sc​(𝐆1)=1.66S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1})=1.66. With 16 impurities Sc​(𝐆1)S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1}) is 0.50.5–0.60.6 in both families and both realizations, below the value of the clean rs=20r_{s}=20 liquid; with 8 impurities it is 0.80.8–1.01.0. Realization 16B at rs=50r_{s}=50 retains a large static star (Sst=1.7S_{\mathrm{st}}=1.7–2.12.1) and a visibly deformed local lattice around the pinned spots, with the highest all-electron ⟨|ψ6|⟩\langle|\psi_{6}|\rangle of the data set (0.410.41–0.420.42, the clean crystal value being 0.430.43); this is what a pinned, deformed Wigner crystal looks like, and it is the one case in model (i) where the structure beyond the impurity sites is organized by the interaction. Its connected star is nevertheless 0.50.5: the positions are pinned, the coherence is gone. Its unbound-electron bond order is 0.340.34, the liquid value. Where the trial families disagree at rs=50r_{s}=50 (PW below PG in energy for the 8-impurity cases and for 16B, by 22–4×10−4​Ha∗4\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}), they disagree about how much static lattice remains, not about the connected part, which is the same in both.

The conclusion of model (i) is foreseeable from the energy scales and the calculation confirms it in every detail at every density: strong point-like charged disorder converts a liquid into a density image with Ni/2N_{i}/2 resolved electrons at the impurity positions, leaves the remaining electrons a liquid that is slightly less correlated than before, and converts an incipient or fully formed crystal into a pinned, deformed texture with no coherent Bragg star. At no density and in no family does it create crystalline correlations that were not there.

3.3 From perturbative to trapping disorder: the impurity-strength scan at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, 50

Model (i) is the strong-coupling limit, and one may object that it answers a question nobody asked: with wells fifty times deeper than e2/ae^{2}/a, of course the impurities win. Model (ii) answers the question that is asked. We fix landscape 16A and scan the impurity charge from Z=1/50Z=1/50, where the impurity binding energy ∼2​Z2\sim 2Z^{2} is a hundred times smaller than e2/ae^{2}/a and the bound-orbit radius ∼aB∗/2​Z\sim a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}/2Z is comparable to aa, to Z=1Z=1, at each of the four densities. At Z≃0.1Z\simeq 0.1–0.20.2 the two energies cross; this is the regime in which a disorder-assisted crystallization, if it existed, would have to show up. The free-center family FG is included so that it can. Figures 14–18 and Table 4 give the results. The four densities answer four different versions of the question: rs=10r_{s}=10 is a liquid far from crystallization, rs=20r_{s}=20 is the density of the imaging experiments, rs=30r_{s}=30 is just below the crystallization point of the polarized system (the clean lattice-Gaussian state is already the lower-energy clean state there, by 1×10−4​Ha∗1\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}, with a static star of 0.980.98 from its own lattice), and rs=50r_{s}=50 is the clean crystal.

The response is approximately quadratic in ZZ over the measured interval Z=0.02Z=0.02–0.20.2. The energy gain relative to the clean state of the same trial family grows by about two decades across this interval, consistent with a linear-response polarization law to within statistical and finite-system scatter (Fig. 17, first column): at rs=20r_{s}=20 from 5×10−55\times 10^{-5} to 1×10−2​Ha∗1\times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}, at rs=30r_{s}=30 from 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} to 1.3×10−2​Ha∗1.3\times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}, at rs=50r_{s}=50 from 1×10−41\times 10^{-4} to 1.5×10−2​Ha∗1.5\times 10^{-2}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}. We quote this as approximate rather than exact: fitted exponents from a straight-line log–log fit over the five sampled ZZ values lie within approximately ±0.2\pm 0.2 of 2 in all three families at all four densities within statistical uncertainty, and a departure from this response is not resolved within the measured range. The departure to the strong-coupling regime occurs only between Z=0.2Z=0.2 and Z=1Z=1, where the gain jumps to 0.170.17–0.20​Ha∗0.20\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} per electron, which is the hydrogenic binding of model (i). Within the sampled interval and the trial-wave-function families used, no change of state consistent with disorder-selected crystallization is seen; approximate quadratic lowering in a finite variational system is not, of course, a general exclusion test.

Weak-disorder changes are small or unresolved; clear suppression of the connected crystalline correlation sets in at Z≳0.1Z\gtrsim 0.1. In the lowest-energy family, Sc​(𝐆1)S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1}) runs, for Z=0Z=0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 1: at rs=10r_{s}=10, 1.111.11, 1.131.13, 1.131.13, 1.111.11, 1.031.03, 0.580.58; at rs=20r_{s}=20, 1.211.21, 1.221.22, 1.191.19, 1.151.15, 0.890.89, 0.470.47; at rs=30r_{s}=30, 1.211.21, 1.211.21, 1.191.19, 1.091.09, 0.760.76, 0.500.50; at rs=50r_{s}=50, 1.181.18, 1.161.16, 1.111.11, 0.960.96, 0.620.62, 0.530.53 (Fig. 17, second column; Table 4). At Z≤0.05Z\leq 0.05 the values track the clean reference within ∼0.02\sim 0.02 at every density, which is within the statistical and finite-system scatter and is consistent with either weak enhancement or weak suppression; from Z=0.1Z=0.1 on every density loses connected weight, and the loss is largest where there was most to lose, at rs=50r_{s}=50, where the clean crystal’s star is reduced by half at Z=0.2Z=0.2. The maximum of Sc​(𝐪)S_{c}(\mathbf{q}) over all wave vectors, which would detect a crystal of any orientation, follows the same course and remains at the pristine star until it is no longer a maximum at all. The static part grows at every density. The local bond order (third column) is unchanged within ±0.003\pm 0.003 at Z≤0.05Z\leq 0.05 and then decreases: at Z=0.2Z=0.2 it is 0.3590.359, 0.3560.356, 0.3560.356, 0.3470.347 at the four densities, against clean values of 0.3680.368, 0.3800.380, 0.3960.396, 0.4320.432. The pair correlation (Fig. 18) loses height at its first peak and the correlation hole fills in as ZZ increases, at every density; at rs=30r_{s}=30 and 50 the shells of the clean (incipient) crystal are gone by Z=0.2Z=0.2. At Z=1Z=1 the pair correlation has a large peak at r≃4​aB∗r\simeq 4a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} from two electrons bound to two adjacent attractive impurities; their mutual repulsion e2/4​aB∗=0.25​Ha∗e^{2}/4a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}=0.25\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} is smaller than their binding, and for them the interaction has become irrelevant.

The disorder-adapted family is the lowest in energy wherever the disorder matters, and it is the least crystalline. From Z=0.05Z=0.05 on, the FG family, whose orbital centers are obtained from a classical minimization in the disorder potential with a prescribed Gaussian smearing and then frozen during VMC optimization of the remaining Jastrow and impurity-factor parameters (Appendix A), has the lowest energy of the three at every density (Table 4), by margins that grow with ZZ and with rsr_{s}: at Z=0.2Z=0.2 by 4×10−44\times 10^{-4}, 1.0×10−31.0\times 10^{-3}, 1.9×10−31.9\times 10^{-3}, 3.2×10−3​Ha∗3.2\times 10^{-3}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} per electron at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, 50 (statistical errors 44–6×10−56\times 10^{-5}). The electrons do prefer to adapt their positional structure to the disorder, and they prefer it most where the clean system is most crystalline. The adapted state has the lowest connected star and the lowest local bond order of the three families at every density where it wins: at Z=0.2Z=0.2, Sc​(𝐆1)=1.03S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1})=1.03, 0.890.89, 0.760.76, 0.620.62 in FG against 1.041.04–1.081.08, 0.970.97–1.031.03, 0.930.93–1.001.00, 0.900.90–1.041.04 in PW and PG. Within the variational space the present family explores, the freedom that would have allowed a disorder-selected crystal to appear is used instead to follow the impurities, and the resulting state has lower connected lattice weight and lower local bond order than the clean ground state in the same family. This bears on the comparison with the local liquid–solid competition under weak short-range disorder analyzed by Joy and Skinner [18]: within the specific trial-wave-function families and disorder models studied here (fixed-charge Coulomb impurities at setback aB∗a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}), the branch that gains most variational energy from the disorder is the branch whose density tracks the impurities rather than a disorder-selected lattice. The models of Ref. [18] and of the present calculation are distinct in disorder spectrum and in the family of competing states considered; the agreement or disagreement between the two theoretical pictures must therefore be discussed in matched models, not read off from the present finite-system numerics.

Pinning sets in at Z≃0.2Z\simeq 0.2 at every density. The number of electrons within 3​aB∗3a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} of the eight attractive impurities rises from the uniform value (72/rs272/r_{s}^{2}) by a factor of 1.11.1–22 at Z=0.02Z=0.02, 1.21.2–4.54.5 at Z=0.05Z=0.05, 1.61.6–1414 at Z=0.1Z=0.1, 33–7676 at Z=0.2Z=0.2 (the larger factors at the lower densities, where the uniform value is smallest), and reaches 6.96.9–7.07.0, one electron per impurity, at Z=1Z=1 (Fig. 17, fourth column). At Z=0.2Z=0.2 the density develops the first resolvable bright spots at the attractive sites and the first depletion around the repulsive ones (Fig. 14); by Z=1Z=1 there are eight spots and eight holes at every density. The onset of a “solid-looking” image coincides with the onset of trapping and with the steepest decline of ScS_{c}, at all four densities. Realization 16B at rs=20r_{s}=20, Z=0.1Z=0.1 (Table 4) has a larger static star than 16A (0.50.5–0.60.6 versus 0.30.3 in the Gaussian families) because its impurity positions happen to correlate better with the reference lattice; its connected star is the same, 1.141.14–1.151.15, below the clean value. The static part depends on the landscape; the connected part does not.

Two numbers in Table 4 could be misread and should be read correctly. At rs=30r_{s}=30 and 5050 the FG and PG bond orders at Z≤0.05Z\leq 0.05 (0.3960.396–0.3980.398 and 0.4240.424–0.4350.435) exceed the clean PW values (0.3800.380 and 0.3920.392); the clean PW state is not the clean ground state at those densities, and compared with the clean state of lowest energy (PG, 0.3960.396 and 0.4320.432) the disordered values are equal within 0.0030.003 or lower. There is no ZZ, at any density, at which any family has a connected star or a bond order above the clean ground state by more than the statistical scatter.

Model (ii) therefore shows what model (i) could not: there is no intermediate disorder strength, at any density from the liquid through the crystallization point to the crystal, at which charged impurities enhance crystalline correlations. The system responds perturbatively, then it traps. The density image becomes more solid-looking at exactly the point where the many-body crystalline correlation starts its steepest decline, and that point is set by the ratio of the impurity binding energy to e2/ae^{2}/a, which is the same Z≃0.2Z\simeq 0.2 at every rsr_{s} studied.

3.4 Donor-layer disorder: liquid, puddles, and the amorphous solid

Point charges one Bohr radius from the plane are the short-range limit of charged disorder. The long-range limit is a layer of remote ionized donors, which in a modulation-doped structure are also the source of the electrons and neutralize them. Model (iii) is this system: 16 electrons, 16 donors of charge +1+1 at the positions of landscape A, at setback dd, computed at d=1d=1, 5, 10, and 20​aB∗20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} for each of the four densities. The resulting potential is smooth on the scale dd, and the natural objects in it, when dd is comparable to the donor spacing, are the puddles of nonlinear screening theory [37], whose connectivity controls the semiclassical percolation transport of low-density 2D systems [25]. Figures 19–23 and Table 5 give the results; the FG family has the lowest energy in every case but two (rs=20r_{s}=20, d=20​aB∗d=20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} and rs=30r_{s}=30, d=aB∗d=a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, where PW is lower by <1×10−4​Ha∗<1\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*}, within the statistical error), by 11–24×10−4​Ha∗24\times 10^{-4}\,\mathrm{Ha}^{*} per electron.

The sixteen panels of Fig. 19 are the central result, because they contain the whole crossover in one place and because the control parameter is visible by inspection: the state depends on d/ad/a, which increases to the right and decreases downward, and not on rsr_{s} alone.

d=aB∗d=a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}: the trapping limit at every density. At d=aB∗d=a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} a donor is a point charge and binds an electron hydrogenically, exactly as the attractive impurities of model (i) do. At all four densities 15.415.4–16.016.0 of the 16 electrons sit within a/4a/4 of a donor, at an rms distance of 1.91.9–2.1​aB∗2.1a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} (the same orbit as in Fig. 13), 8383–98%98\% of the cell is below n¯/2\bar{n}/2, and the connected star is 0.260.26, 0.080.08, 0.030.03, 0.010.01 at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, 30, 50, against clean values of 1.11.1–1.21.2. The donor energy is seven to forty times the electron–electron energy. The density image is sixteen spots at the sixteen donor positions, at every density; the structure factor is entirely static. This column is the n/ni=1n/n_{i}=1 version of model (i), and it is the state to which the entire grid flows as d/a→0d/a\to 0.

rs=10r_{s}=10: from trapped to liquid as the setback grows. Along the top row, d/a=0.05d/a=0.05, 0.260.26, 0.530.53, 1.051.05. At d=10​aB∗d=10a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} the occupied region is 72%72\% of the cell, spanning, with maximum density 3.6​n¯3.6\bar{n}, no static star (0.010.01), and Sc​(𝐆1)=0.95S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1})=0.95; at d=20​aB∗d=20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} it is 82%82\%, the static star is zero, and Sc​(𝐆1)=1.03S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1})=1.03, within 10%10\% of the clean liquid. The local bond order is 0.350.35–0.360.36 throughout, at or just below the clean 0.370.37. This row is the puddle regime of a high-density sample: the landscape is smooth, the liquid fills the valleys and spans the cell, and the electron–electron energy exceeds the donor energy from d=5​aB∗d=5a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} on.

The clean Wigner crystal at rs=50r_{s}=50 does not exist as a correlated object in this model at any setback up to 20​aB∗20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}.

The crossover is set by d/ad/a, i.e., by n/nin/n_{i} and the disorder length, not by rcr_{c}. Reading Fig. 19 along a column, lowering the density at fixed setback takes the system from a connected liquid through isolated puddles to one electron per donor; reading it along a row, increasing the setback at fixed density does the reverse. The states with the same d/ad/a look alike: (rs=10,d=5​aB∗)(r_{s}=10,d=5a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}), (rs=20,d=10​aB∗)(r_{s}=20,d=10a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}), and (rs=50,d=20​aB∗)(r_{s}=50,d=20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}), with d/a=0.26d/a=0.26, 0.260.26, 0.210.21, have Sc​(𝐆1)=0.83S_{c}(\mathbf{G}_{1})=0.83, 0.510.51, 0.150.15 — a sequence that reflects the increasing dominance of the donor energy over the interaction energy as rsr_{s} grows, not any crystalline tendency, since the local bond order is 0.350.35–0.370.37 in all three. The solid-looking state appears at rs≈20r_{s}\approx 20 for d=10​aB∗d=10a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} because that is where aa exceeds ∼3\sim 3–44 times dd and the smooth landscape resolves into individual wells; with d=5​aB∗d=5a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} it appears at rs≈10r_{s}\approx 10–2020 and with d=20​aB∗d=20a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*} at rs≈30r_{s}\approx 30. This is the n/nin/n_{i} argument of Sec. 1 realized in a calculation: the construction holds NN and NiN_{i} fixed and uses the same fractional impurity coordinates as the cell is rescaled with rsr_{s}, so that ni/nn_{i}/n is held fixed at unity throughout while the physical nn and nin_{i} both change together; lowering rsr_{s} then takes the system monotonically from a liquid-side state through puddles to one electron per impurity, with the connected crystalline correlation decreasing at every step, at every setback. This is a fixed-ni/nn_{i}/n, variable-d/ad/a path through parameter space; it is not an experimental fixed-sample gate sweep in which nin_{i} is held constant and nn is varied, which would require a different cell construction.
