    On the mechanism of the 2D MIT in Si and GaAs [21], the half-depletion density n1/2n_{1/2} of the semiclassical nonlinear-Thomas–Fermi landscape and the Ioffe–Regel–Mott density nIRMn_{\mathrm{IRM}} of Born–RPA transport are reached at the common energetic condition Edis∼EFE_{\mathrm{dis}}\sim E_{F} (Sec. 5); the two scales track each other to within a factor of order unity in the long-range-Coulomb model studied, with slow n¯i−1/10d−1/5\bar{n}_{i}^{-1/10}d^{-1/5} spread. Modest independent short-range transport channels can shift the ratio by factors of order two. These statements are made within the specific scope of the two calculations and are not a theorem relating the geometric depletion scale to a true percolation threshold.

  3. 3.

    In the magnetized collective-pinning picture of Ref. [33], the microwave pinning-mode resonance of the GaAs 2DEG in strong perpendicular field [47, 48, 49] sits at ωp≃ct2/(ωc​Rc2)\omega_{p}\simeq c_{t}^{2}/(\omega_{c}R_{c}^{2}) when ωc≫ω0\omega_{c}\gg\omega_{0}. Combined with the two weak-pinning Larkin scalings of Sec. 6, this gives parametric expectations ωp∝W2\omega_{p}\propto W^{2} in an HF disorder-amplitude scan and ωp∝n¯i\omega_{p}\propto\bar{n}_{i} in a classical concentration scan, within the collective weak-pinning regime. Both the identification of the first-shell density-coherence length with the Larkin length and the extrapolation of weak-pinning elasticity into the strong-pinning regime require independent verification before these parametric statements can be used quantitatively.

Open questions include the thermodynamic-limit extrapolation of the coherence length from the present finite-cell calculations, the role of spin and valley degeneracies in the amorphous solid, the competition between the amorphous solid and the fractional quantum Hall liquid in the LLL [30, 57] at specific rational fillings, the finite-temperature phase diagram of the pinned amorphous solid, and the extension of the analysis to systems with screening by nearby gates and to electron-hole bilayers. The methodology of this paper—organized around the dimensionless disorder-to-electron density ratio n¯i/n\bar{n}_{i}/n, with the Imry–Ma–Larkin picture as the structural framework and with HF, VMC, LLL HF, and nonlinear-TF as the complementary microscopic tools—is directly applicable to each of these extensions.

Appendix A Variational Monte Carlo computational details

A.1 Computational details

Cell and lattice. The rhombic cell has primitive vectors (L,0)(L,0) and (L/2,3​L/2)(L/2,\sqrt{3}L/2) with L=4​aL=4a and a=1.90463​rs​aB∗a=1.90463\,r_{s}a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*}, area π​N​rs2​(aB∗)2\pi Nr_{s}^{2}(a_{\mathrm{B}}^{*})^{2}; it contains a 4×44\times 4 triangular lattice whose first reciprocal star {𝐆1}\{\mathbf{G}_{1}\} has |𝐆1|=4​π/3​a|\mathbf{G}_{1}|=4\pi/\sqrt{3}a. Structure factors are evaluated at all reciprocal vectors 𝐪=m​𝐛1+n​𝐛2\mathbf{q}=m\mathbf{b}_{1}+n\mathbf{b}_{2} with |m|,|n|≤8|m|,|n|\leq 8. Electron–electron and electron–impurity interactions are 2D Ewald sums with the impurity plane offset by dd; the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 background terms are constants and are omitted (so ⟨Vimp⟩\langle V_{\rm imp}\rangle for the donor layer is defined up to a constant that depends on rsr_{s} and dd).

Trial functions and optimization. The plane-wave determinant uses the 13 lowest closed-shell momenta plus a zero-total-momentum triplet at the fourth shell. The Gaussian orbitals are ϕβ(𝐫)=∑𝐓exp[−β|𝐫−𝐓|2/2]\phi_{\beta}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{T}}\exp[-\beta|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{T}|^{2}/2] over lattice translations 𝐓\mathbf{T}, with one common optimized width. The Jastrow is U=∑i<ja​ri​j/(1+b​ri​j)U=\sum_{i<j}a\,r_{ij}/(1+b\,r_{ij}) with aa fixed by the cusp condition for the polarized system and bb optimized. The impurity factor has three parameters (κ+\kappa_{+}, κ−\kappa_{-}, ℓ\ell); for the donor layer κ−\kappa_{-} is inert. The impurity Coulomb singularity needs no regularization: the electron–impurity cusp is carried by WW, the local energy is finite at coincidence, and the 2D Ewald kernel is integrable. Parameters are optimized by stochastic reconfiguration with 40–60 iterations of 64 blocks each, 16 chains, with the impurity amplitudes initialized proportional to ZZ; the final parameters are the average over the last 8–10 iterations. For the FG family the orbital centers are obtained by L-BFGS minimization of the classical energy of 16 point charges in the Ewald electron–electron potential plus the impurity potential convolved with the Gaussian orbital density |ϕβ|2|\phi_{\beta}|^{2} (evaluated in reciprocal space, with β\beta taken from the clean PG optimization at the same rsr_{s}), from 13 starting arrangements (the lattice, six lattice-plus-noise, six random), keeping the lowest; the centers are then frozen and β\beta, bb, κ±\kappa_{\pm}, ℓ\ell are optimized by VMC as for the other families. For Z≤0.05Z\leq 0.05 the relaxed centers are within 0.02​a0.02a of the lattice sites; for Z=1Z=1 and for the donor layer they sit on or between the attractive impurities.

Sampling. Production uses 24 Markov chains, 1200 blocks of 32 single-electron Metropolis sweeps with mixed local and global (impurity-centered) proposals and full Hastings ratios, after 120 equilibration blocks; every state yields 28 800 stored configurations from which all diagnostics are computed. Quoted errors are the larger of the chain-to-chain standard error and the plateau of a time-reblocking analysis. Sampler correctness was verified against known targets and the local energy against finite-difference Laplacians of the full wave function at configurations including an electron inside an impurity core. The one-body densities are 96×9696\times 96 histograms on the fractional cell; the sixfold bond order uses the six nearest minimum-image neighbors; the spanning test for the donor layer is a periodic connected-component analysis of the thresholded density on a 3×33\times 3 tiling of the cell.

Data. The model (i) results at rs=10r_{s}=10, 20, and 50 and the pristine references at those densities were generated in an earlier stage of the project with the same code, and their stored production configurations were re-analyzed for this paper; every other state (the rs=30r_{s}=30 references and all rs=30r_{s}=30 disordered states, the complete model (ii) scans at four densities, the complete model (iii) grid of four setbacks at four densities, and the FG family throughout), the static/connected decomposition, the bound/unbound split, and the bond-order and morphology analyses were generated here from the same Hamiltonian and sampler. All results in the tables are from the stored production configurations. In all, 139 VMC ground states were computed and analyzed.

Appendix B Lowest Landau level HF — disorder landscape and puddle picture

This appendix collects the computational details of the LLL landscape and puddle analyses summarized in Sec. 4: the form of the impurity landscape, its filling by lakes and puddles, the behavior on a larger sample, where the Hartree–Fock electrons sit on it, how well they screen it, how it changes with the impurity setback, and the Hartree-deletion numerical experiment. The Hartree-deletion calculation is a controlled diagnostic that isolates the role of electrostatic stiffness in the full theory: it is one route by which density inhomogeneity becomes favorable in a model Hamiltonian, not a claim that physical puddles can arise only when Hartree repulsion is removed. Both the Thomas–Fermi calculations of Sec. 5 and the VMC donor-layer calculations of Sec. 3 produce density puddles with full Hartree repulsion retained. Within the LLL–HF search explored here, however, the full solution does not approach a filled-droplet state at any filling studied, and the structural interpretation developed in Sec. 4.5 follows.

B.0.1 The potential landscape seen by a test electron

The one-body impurity term is Eq. (21). Written in real space it is the potential energy

V(𝐫)=1A∑𝐪≠0V(𝐪)e−q2ℓ2/4ei​𝐪⋅𝐫V(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\mathbf{q}\neq 0}V(\mathbf{q})\,e^{-q^{2}\ell^{2}/4}\,e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}} (62)

of a test electron, with V⁡(𝐪)V(\mathbf{q}) from Eq. (20). It carries the same Landau level form factor e−q2ℓ2/4e^{-q^{2}\ell^{2}/4} that enters the matrix elements, so that structure finer than a magnetic length is absent, as it must be for an electron confined to the lowest level. Figure 34(a) shows this landscape for the sample used throughout the paper, Ni=80N_{i}=80 charges of both signs at setback d=6​ℓd=6\ell, and Fig. 34(b) shows the same function in relief, which is the form in which the hills and basins are easiest to read.

The amplitude is Vrms=0.1485​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)V_{\rm rms}=0.1485\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell) and the extreme values on this sample are −0.283-0.283 and +0.349​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)+0.349\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell). For comparison, the clean condensation energy per electron is 0.130​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)0.130\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell) at ν=1/2\nu=1/2 and at most 0.197​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)0.197\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell) near ν=0.21\nu=0.21. The landscape is therefore not a weak perturbation: its typical excursion is of the same order as the energy that holds the crystal together, and its extremes are larger.

The landscape is also smooth, and this is the property that matters most for what follows. Its autocorrelation function falls to one half at 7.2​ℓ7.2\,\ell and first crosses zero at 12.2​ℓ12.2\,\ell for d=6​ℓd=6\ell; at d=3​ℓd=3\ell the corresponding numbers are 6.1​ℓ6.1\,\ell and 11.8​ℓ11.8\,\ell. This is the precise sense in which Coulomb disorder is slowly varying, and it is intrinsic rather than incidental: a charged impurity at a setback dd produces a basin whose width is set by dd and by the Coulomb tail, and no choice of impurity density changes that width. Only the amplitude responds to the impurity density, through the usual Ni\sqrt{N_{i}} of a random superposition.

What does change with filling is the length the landscape is being compared with. The lattice constant of the crystal, a=ℓ​4​π/(3​ν)a=\ell\sqrt{4\pi/(\sqrt{3}\,\nu)}, grows from 3.81​ℓ3.81\,\ell at ν=1/2\nu=1/2 through 4.76​ℓ4.76\,\ell at ν=0.32\nu=0.32 and 6.35​ℓ6.35\,\ell at ν=0.18\nu=0.18 to 8.52​ℓ8.52\,\ell at ν=0.10\nu=0.10. Measured in crystal sites, a region of the correlation area π​ξV2\pi\xi_{V}^{2} with ξV=7.2​ℓ\xi_{V}=7.2\,\ell contains about 1313 sites at ν=1/2\nu=1/2, 88 at ν=0.32\nu=0.32, 55 at ν=0.18\nu=0.18 and 2.62.6 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10. A basin that at half filling accommodates a coherent patch of a dozen crystal sites accommodates two or three at the lowest filling. In the first case the disorder acts on the crystal collectively, displacing a patch that remains internally ordered; in the second it acts on individual electrons. This is an independent reason, additional to the growth of ni/nn_{i}/n, for the collapse of the crystalline coherence length documented in Sec. 4.4, and the two act in the same direction.

B.0.2 Filling the landscape: the lake construction

The semiclassical construction is the obvious one and we use it only as a reference, not as an approximation we believe. Let μν\mu_{\nu} be the level whose sub-level set V⁡(𝐫)<μνV(\mathbf{r})<\mu_{\nu} covers an area fraction ν\nu, and call that sub-level set the lake. Electrons that filled the landscape to a waterline while ignoring one another entirely would occupy the lake exactly, with local filling one inside it and zero outside. Figures 34(c)–(f) show the lake at ν=0.50\nu=0.50, 0.320.32, 0.180.18 and 0.100.10.

Table 11 gives the construction in full on the paper’s own sample. The waterline μν\mu_{\nu} falls monotonically from +0.085​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)+0.085\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell) at ν=0.70\nu=0.70 to −0.191​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)-0.191\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell) at ν=0.10\nu=0.10, as it must. The lake remains a single connected region at every filling down to ν=0.10\nu=0.10; the entire lake area is always in one component. What does change is that below ν≃0.40\nu\simeq 0.40 the lake no longer winds around the torus, so that a path through the lake can no longer traverse the sample.

This must not be over-read. The sample is 38×33​ℓ38\times 33\,\ell and contains 8080 impurities, which on a landscape with a correlation length of 7​ℓ7\,\ell amounts to a handful of hills and a handful of basins. A single-component lake down to ν=0.10\nu=0.10 is a statement about this particular small sample and not about the statistics of such landscapes. We therefore repeated the construction on larger samples, which is the subject of the next subsection.

B.0.3 Larger samples, and why we quote no threshold

We generated landscapes at the same impurity density, ni=0.0637​ℓ−2n_{i}=0.0637\,\ell^{-2}, on a torus five times larger in area, A=6283​ℓ2A=6283\,\ell^{2} with Ni=400N_{i}=400 impurities, at both setbacks. Table 12 gives the connectivity of the lake there, and the bottom row of Fig. 35 shows it for d=3​ℓd=3\ell.

Now the lake does break up. At d=3​ℓd=3\ell it goes from one component at ν≥0.40\nu\geq 0.40 — but for a single detached speck at ν=0.50\nu=0.50, which leaves 0.9940.994 of the lake area in the main body — to 33, 44, 77 and 88 disconnected puddles at ν=0.32\nu=0.32, 0.180.18, 0.120.12 and 0.100.10, and the fraction of the lake area carried by its largest component falls to 0.2450.245. At d=6​ℓd=6\ell the same trend is present but weaker, reaching 33 puddles and a largest-component fraction of 0.6590.659 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10, which is what one expects of a smoother landscape with fewer and broader basins. These larger samples are illustrative: no Hartree–Fock solution was computed on them, and they appear here only to show what the same landscape statistics do when given room.

It is tempting to look for a threshold in these numbers. We deliberately do not quote one, and the reason is worth recording because we tested it. For a statistically symmetric random field in two dimensions, a self-duality argument places the connectivity threshold of the level set at area fraction exactly one half, which would make ν=1/2\nu=1/2 a special filling. Equal numbers of positive and negative impurities ought to produce such a symmetric field. They do not, on these samples: the measured skewness of VV is +0.289+0.289 on the paper’s own sample at d=6​ℓd=6\ell and +0.335+0.335 at d=3​ℓd=3\ell, and +0.336+0.336 and +0.182+0.182 on the five-times larger samples. Nor is the behavior consistent with a one-half threshold in any case: on the large d=3​ℓd=3\ell sample the lake still spans at ν=0.60\nu=0.60 and is already fragmented at ν=0.32\nu=0.32, with spanning lost between ν=0.60\nu=0.60 and ν=0.55\nu=0.55, while on the paper’s own sample it survives to ν=0.40\nu=0.40. The duality argument requires short-range correlations, and the Coulomb potential retains a long tail even at a setback, so its level sets are not generic in the required sense. We therefore report the connectivity as measured and attach no threshold to it.

B.0.4 Where the Hartree–Fock electrons actually sit

The dots in Figs. 34(c)–(f) are the density maxima of the converged Hartree–Fock solution at the same filling, on the same sample, with the same impurities, taken from the production runs of Sec. 4.4. At ν=0.50\nu=0.50 they cover the sample in a crystal that takes almost no notice of the shoreline. At ν=0.10\nu=0.10 they have moved into the basins. Table 13 makes this quantitative with three independent measures, each given for all three impurity numbers.

The first is the correlation coefficient between the density n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}) and the landscape V⁡(𝐫)V(\mathbf{r}) over the whole sample. It is negative at every filling, as it should be if electrons prefer basins, and it strengthens from −0.180-0.180 at ν=0.50\nu=0.50 to −0.249-0.249 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 for Ni=80N_{i}=80. Its filling dependence is not monotonic: it weakens to −0.137-0.137 near ν=0.28\nu=0.28 before growing again. The reason is that this coefficient is diluted by the crystal’s own density modulation, which is large and has nothing to do with the disorder, and that modulation is strongest in the middle of the filling range where the condensation energy peaks. For this reason we regard it as the least clean of the three measures and quote it mainly for completeness.

The second is the mean landscape height at the electron positions, ⟨V⟩el\langle V\rangle_{\rm el}, in units of VrmsV_{\rm rms}. It vanishes for electrons placed without regard to the landscape and is negative for electrons in basins. It is monotonic in filling at every disorder strength, which the correlation coefficient is not, and it is the measure we use in the body of the paper. For Ni=80N_{i}=80 it runs −0.073-0.073, −0.100-0.100, −0.233-0.233, −0.512-0.512 at ν=0.50\nu=0.50, 0.360.36, 0.180.18, 0.100.10; for Ni=56N_{i}=56 and Ni=24N_{i}=24 the corresponding ranges are −0.066-0.066 to −0.445-0.445 and −0.045-0.045 to −0.318-0.318. More disorder traps the electrons more, and lower filling traps them more, with no crossings between the three curves.

The third is the fraction flakef_{\rm lake} of electrons found inside the lake, which would equal ν\nu if the electrons took no notice of it. The ratio flake/νf_{\rm lake}/\nu rises from 1.081.08 at ν=0.50\nu=0.50 to 1.501.50 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 for Ni=80N_{i}=80. This measure is the noisiest of the three because it counts discrete electrons — at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 there are only twenty of them — and it occasionally dips below unity, as at ν=0.18\nu=0.18 for Ni=56N_{i}=56, where flake/ν=0.93f_{\rm lake}/\nu=0.93. The trend is nevertheless unambiguous across all three impurity numbers.

Taken together the three measures say the same thing, and it is a quantitative statement rather than a qualitative one. The trapping is real, it grows monotonically as the filling falls and as the disorder grows, and it is modest. At half filling the crystal is very nearly indifferent to a landscape whose rms is comparable to the condensation energy per electron. Even at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 the electrons sit only half a standard deviation below the mean landscape height, and only fifty percent more of them lie in the lake than chance would put there. Nothing in these numbers resembles a set of filled puddles.

B.0.5 Screening of the landscape

The electrons are not passive on this landscape; they rearrange and screen it. Writing the self-consistent Hartree potential of the electron density as UH​(𝐫)U_{H}(\mathbf{r}), the landscape a test electron actually experiences is V+UHV+U_{H}. Table 14 gives three measures of what the screening does.

The first is the bare ratio Vrmstot/VrmsV^{\rm tot}_{\rm rms}/V_{\rm rms}. At ν=1/2\nu=1/2 it is 0.330.33 for Ni=80N_{i}=80: the electrons flatten the landscape to a third of its bare amplitude. As the filling falls the ratio rises, passes unity near ν≃0.18\nu\simeq 0.18, and reaches 1.161.16 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10. The total landscape is then rougher than the bare one. This sounds like a failure of screening and is not: at low filling the crystal’s own density modulation is nearly complete, the density contrast reaching unity, and the Hartree potential of that modulation is large and has a period set by the lattice and not by the disorder. The ratio is contaminated by the crystal’s own field and we quote it only to explain why a second measure is needed.

The second is the projection of the total landscape onto the bare one,

α=⟨(V+UH)​V⟩⟨V2⟩,\alpha=\frac{\langle(V+U_{H})\,V\rangle}{\langle V^{2}\rangle}, (63)

which removes the part of UHU_{H} that is uncorrelated with the disorder. It is unity without screening and zero with perfect screening. We find α\alpha negative at every filling and every disorder strength: −0.128-0.128 at ν=1/2\nu=1/2 and −0.450-0.450 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 for Ni=80N_{i}=80, with the same pattern for Ni=24N_{i}=24 and Ni=56N_{i}=56. The electrons do not merely screen the disorder; they overscreen it, and the residual landscape is anticorrelated with the bare one. The magnitude of the overscreening is not monotonic in filling, passing through a minimum between ν=0.32\nu=0.32 and ν=0.36\nu=0.36 before growing strongly at low filling.

The third is the same projection restricted to the slowly varying components q<G1/2q<G_{1}/2, where the disorder has its weight and the crystal Bragg peaks do not. This was computed as a check that the crystal’s own field was not contaminating α\alpha. It is not: the restricted and unrestricted values agree to within a few percent over most of the range and to 9%9\% at worst, the largest discrepancy being −0.458-0.458 against −0.416-0.416 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 for Ni=24N_{i}=24. The overscreening is therefore a property of the long-wavelength response and not an artifact of the Bragg peaks.

Within Hartree–Fock, overscreening is what one should expect. Linear screening with a positive compressibility gives 0<α<10<\alpha<1; a negative α\alpha requires a negative dielectric function, which in this theory follows from the exchange-driven negative compressibility of the lowest Landau level. That it strengthens as the filling falls is consistent with the exchange energy becoming relatively more important as the density drops.

B.0.6 Terrain roughness at the two setbacks

Figures 35(a) and (b) show the same impurity positions at the two setbacks on a common color scale, and Fig. 35(c) shows the stronger landscape in relief. Halving the setback doubles the amplitude, Vrms=0.1485→0.2952​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)V_{\rm rms}=0.1485\to 0.2952\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell), and widens the range from [−0.283,+0.349][-0.283,+0.349] to [−0.738,+0.833]​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)[-0.738,+0.833]\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell). It sharpens the terrain much less: the correlation half-width falls only from 7.2​ℓ7.2\,\ell to 6.1​ℓ6.1\,\ell, and the first zero from 12.2​ℓ12.2\,\ell to 11.8​ℓ11.8\,\ell. Even at the shorter setback the landscape is smooth on the scale of the lattice constant at every filling we study. The setback is therefore mainly an amplitude knob and only weakly a length knob, which is why the two setbacks give the same qualitative physics with shifted thresholds, as reported in Sec. 4.4.4.

B.0.7 Checks on the Hartree potential

Because the sign of α\alpha is the one surprising result in this appendix, we record the checks made on UHU_{H}. It is positive where the density is high, as a repulsive potential must be: the correlation between UH​(𝐫)U_{H}(\mathbf{r}) and n⁡(𝐫)n(\mathbf{r}) is +0.43+0.43 at ν=0.50\nu=0.50 and +0.73+0.73 at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 for the full solution, and +0.90+0.90 for the Hartree-free droplet discussed below. It vanishes identically for the uniform state P=ν​𝕀P=\nu\mathbb{I}, for which all Δ⁡(𝐆≠0)\Delta(\mathbf{G}\neq 0) are zero, with a computed maximum of 00 to machine precision. Its form factors are the same as those of the impurity potential: the physical density already carries one factor e−q2ℓ2/4e^{-q^{2}\ell^{2}/4}, and the test electron that feels the resulting potential carries a second, exactly as in Eq. (62).

B.0.8 Removing the Hartree term

We come to the point of the appendix. The energy functional, Eq. (13), contains the Hartree kernel UH​(G)U_{H}(G) and the exchange kernel X⁡(G)X(G), and only the first penalizes charge inhomogeneity. At the first shell of the ν=1/2\nu=1/2 crystal, G1​ℓ=1.905G_{1}\ell=1.905, the two are UH=+0.0856U_{H}=+0.0856 and X=+0.6156​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)X=+0.6156\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell), giving W=UH−X=−0.5300W=U_{H}-X=-0.5300. Deleting UHU_{H} leaves the kernel −X⁡(G)-X(G), which is negative at every qq and, since XX decreases monotonically, most negative as q→0q\to 0. The sum rule, Eq. (16), continues to require a density-wave weight ν⁡(1−ν)\nu(1-\nu), but there is now no reason not to place all of it at the longest wavelength the sample allows. The expected consequence is phase separation.

That is what happens. Figure 36 compares the two theories on the same sample, with the same impurities, the same solver, the same adiabatic continuation and the same set of starting determinants; the lower row deletes UH​(G)U_{H}(G) from the kernel and changes nothing else. The lower row is the puddle state in its pure form. The electrons collapse into a single droplet that is locally full, 2​π​ℓ2​n=12\pi\ell^{2}n=1, with an edge one magnetic length wide, and the boundary of that droplet coincides with the semiclassical shoreline V=μνV=\mu_{\nu} drawn in red. That contour is computed from the bare landscape alone and has no knowledge of the solution. The electrons fill the lake to the waterline, which is precisely the lake construction of Sec. B.0.2 above.

Table 15 gives the numbers alongside the full calculation. Four features are worth drawing out.

First, the energy per electron without the Hartree term is −0.730-0.730, −0.758-0.758, −0.777-0.777 and −0.777​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)-0.777\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell) at ν=0.50\nu=0.50, 0.320.32, 0.180.18 and 0.100.10. It is almost independent of filling, and that independence is the signature of phase separation: the energy per electron is set by the local density inside the droplet, which is unity, and not by how many electrons the sample contains. The full calculation, by contrast, gives an energy that tracks the filling closely, from −0.449-0.449 to −0.279​(e2/ϵ​ℓ)-0.279\,(e^{2}/\epsilon\ell) over the same range.

Second, the density contrast is exactly unity at every filling without the Hartree term, whereas the full calculation reaches unity only below ν≃0.18\nu\simeq 0.18 and is 0.7490.749 at half filling.

Third, the Bragg-ring weight NeffN_{\rm eff} rises from 9.49.4 to 53.753.7 at ν=1/2\nu=1/2, from 10.410.4 to 55.955.9 at ν=0.32\nu=0.32 and from 20.520.5 to 65.765.7 at ν=0.18\nu=0.18 when the Hartree term is removed. Here NeffN_{\rm eff} must be read with care rather than as a crystallinity scale: a droplet has no crystalline order at all, and the ring weight is simply measuring how far the density has moved from six Bragg spots. At ν=0.10\nu=0.10 the ordering inverts, 38.538.5 for the full solution against 18.118.1 without the Hartree term, because there the full solution is the most amorphous state in the entire study while the droplet is a single compact object whose weight has largely left the ring altogether.

Fourth, the trapping measures saturate. The fraction of electrons in the lake rises to 1.611.61, 3.123.12, 4.174.17 and 4.004.00 times chance, against 1.101.10 to 1.501.50 for the full calculation, and ⟨V⟩el/Vrms\langle V\rangle_{\rm el}/V_{\rm rms} reaches −1.441-1.441 at ν=0.32\nu=0.32, against −0.107-0.107 for the full calculation at the same filling.

Two cautions. These energies are not variational for the true Hamiltonian; they are lower than the full ones only because a positive term has been deleted, and nothing should be inferred from their magnitude. And at ν=0.10\nu=0.10 the droplet contains only twenty electrons; exchange then dominates the landscape on the scale of the droplet, and the droplet no longer settles in the deepest basin, so that ⟨V⟩el\langle V\rangle_{\rm el} turns slightly positive, +0.032+0.032. This is why the lower curve in Fig. 36(d) is not monotonic, and it is why the comparison is most meaningful at the higher fillings where the droplet is large.

Appendix C Thomas–Fermi/IRM computational details

C.1 Computational details (TF/IRM)

C.1.1 Active-set formulation of the local-TF obstacle problem

On a periodic mesh, let 𝒏\bm{n} be the density vector at fixed mean 𝟏T​𝒏=Nsite​n\bm{1}^{T}\bm{n}=N_{\rm site}n. In the local-TF calculation the discrete functional has the form

E⁡(𝒏)=12​𝒏T​(π​I+V)​𝒏+𝑽impT​𝒏+constant,E(\bm{n})=\frac{1}{2}\bm{n}^{T}(\pi I+V)\bm{n}+\bm{V}_{\rm imp}^{T}\bm{n}+\text{constant}, (64)

with 𝒏≥0\bm{n}\geq 0. The matrix VV is the Fourier representation of the Coulomb kernel with its zero mode deleted. On an occupied support SS,

(π​I+V)S​𝒏S+𝑽imp,S=μ​𝟏S.(\pi I+V)_{S}\bm{n}_{S}+\bm{V}_{{\rm imp},S}=\mu\bm{1}_{S}. (65)

Two conjugate-gradient solves give

𝒏S=𝒙S+μ​𝒚S,AS​𝒙S=−𝑽imp,S,AS​𝒚S=𝟏S,\bm{n}_{S}=\bm{x}_{S}+\mu\bm{y}_{S},\quad A_{S}\bm{x}_{S}=-\bm{V}_{{\rm imp},S},\quad A_{S}\bm{y}_{S}=\bm{1}_{S}, (66)

and the density constraint fixes

μ=Nsite​n−𝟏ST​𝒙S𝟏ST​𝒚S.\mu=\frac{N_{\rm site}n-\bm{1}_{S}^{T}\bm{x}_{S}}{\bm{1}_{S}^{T}\bm{y}_{S}}. (67)

The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions require positive density on SS and (π​I+V)​𝒏+𝑽imp≥μ(\pi I+V)\bm{n}+\bm{V}_{\rm imp}\geq\mu outside it. Updating SS until these inequalities stabilize solves the nonlinear depletion problem without smearing the density support. The classical check is obtained by replacing π​I\pi I by zero on a nontrivial support.

C.1.2 Derivation of the transport quadrature and remote-scattering limit

The radial k′k^{\prime} integral in Eq. (47) gives the two-dimensional density of final states. With t=θ/2t=\theta/2, one has q=2​kF​sin⁡tq=2k_{F}\sin t, 1−cos⁡θ=2​sin2⁡t1-\cos\theta=2\sin^{2}t, and d​θ=2​d​td\theta=2dt. Substitution of Eq. (45) then gives Eq. (48). The equality ρ/(h/e2)=1/(kF​ℓ)\rho/(h/e^{2})=1/(k_{F}\ell) follows from σ=n​e2​τt/m=(e2/h)​kF​ℓ\sigma=ne^{2}\tau_{t}/m=(e^{2}/h)k_{F}\ell for gs=2g_{s}=2.

For kF​d≫1k_{F}d\gg 1, set sin⁡t≃t\sin t\simeq t in the forward-scattering region. The leading integral is

∫0∞d​t​t2​e−4​kF​d​t=132​kF3​d3,\int_{0}^{\infty}dt\,t^{2}e^{-4k_{F}dt}=\frac{1}{32k_{F}^{3}d^{3}}, (68)

which produces Eq. (50). This derivation explains why the IRM scale can drop faster with dd than the classical real-space percolation scale.

C.1.3 Short-range transport contribution

For the effective correlator in Eq. (57), the angular average of 1−cos⁡θ1-\cos\theta is unity. Equation (47) therefore gives

1τsr=m​Wsrℏ3.\frac{1}{\tau_{\rm sr}}=\frac{mW_{\rm sr}}{\hbar^{3}}. (69)

Combining this result with ρ=m/(n​e2​τt)\rho=m/(ne^{2}\tau_{t}) and h=2​π​ℏh=2\pi\hbar yields Eq. (58). Thus γsr\gamma_{\rm sr} has a direct operational meaning: in the absence of remote disorder, the white-noise component alone reaches ρ=h/e2\rho=h/e^{2} at n​aB2=γsrna_{\rm B}^{2}=\gamma_{\rm sr}. This is a transport parameter, not an additional long-distance percolation parameter.

C.1.4 Scope of the crossover function

The numerical F1/2​(x)F_{1/2}(x) is a controlled output of a local Hartree-TF functional with continuum Gaussian disorder. It does not include exchange and correlation corrections to the compressibility, nonlocal density response, finite quantum-well width, correlated impurities, quantum tunneling between puddles, or interference localization. The large-xx agreement with EPB validates the correct classical limit of this model. The finite-xx values should instead be interpreted as a quantitatively useful local-TF crossover benchmark. A microscopic small-dd prediction requires specifying the ultraviolet physics omitted here.
